Surah al-Ankabut (The Spider)

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was revealed in Mecca. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr something similar to that. The view that it is Meccan has also been reported from al-Hasan, Jabir and 'Ikrimah, and from some of them that it was the last thing revealed in Mecca. In al-Bahr, from al-Habr (Ibn 'Abbas) and Qatadah, it is reported that it is Medinan. Yahya ibn Salam said: it is Meccan except from its beginning up to His saying: ﴿And Allah will surely make evident the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ankabut: 11]. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned this in al-Itqan without attributing it. He said that when Ibn Jarir included it in the reasons for its revelation, he then said: I say, to this should be added ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision﴾ [al-Ankabut: 60] and the verse, because of what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning the reason for its revelation; and the discussion of that will come, Allah willing. It has sixty-nine verses by consensus, as al-Dani and al-Tabarsi said.

Al-Jalal mentioned, regarding its connection to what precedes it, that in the beginning of the previous surah Allah informed about Pharaoh that he ﴿exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, weakening a group among them: he slaughtered their sons and spared their women﴾ [al-Qasas: 4]. This surah opens with mention of the believers whom the disbelievers tried and tormented for their faith, with a torment less than what Pharaoh inflicted on the Children of Israel by much, as consolation for them with what befell those before them and as encouragement to patience. For this reason it is said here: ﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-Ankabut: 3]. Also, since the end of the first surah contained an allusion to the Prophet's emigration (ﷺ), namely in His saying: ﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas: 85], according to some views, and at the end of this surah there is an allusion to the emigration of the believers in His saying: ﴿O My servants who have believed, indeed My earth is spacious﴾ [al-Ankabut: 56], their sequence was appropriate.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ The discussion of it and its counterparts has already passed. Some scholars did not permit here the connection of what follows it as a grammatical (i'rabi) connection, because the interrogative prevents it. This was examined: the requirement regarding the interrogative is that it begin its clause, and this does not preclude that clause occurring as a predicate (khabar) and the like, such as your saying: Zayd, has his father stood up? ﴿أحَسِبَ النّاسُ﴾ إلى آخِرِ السُّورَةِ صَحَّ، فَلا يُقالُ أيْضًا إنَّ المانِعَ مِنهُ عَدَمُ صِحَّةِ ارْتِباطِهِ بِما قَبْلَهُ مَعْنًى. نَعَمِ، الِارْتِباطُ خِلافُ الظّاهِرِ، والِاسْتِفْهامُ لِلْإنْكارِ، والحُسْبانُ مَصْدَرٌ كالغُفْرانِ، مِمّا يَتَعَلَّقُ بِمَضامِينِ الجُمَلِ، لِأنَّهُ مِنَ الأفْعالِ الدّاخِلَةِ عَلى المُبْتَدَأِ (المبتدأ: الاسم المرفوع الذي يبدأ به الكلام) والخَبَرِ (الخبر: ما يُسند إلى المبتدأ)، وذَلِكَ لِلدَّلالَةِ عَلى وجْهِ ثُبُوتِها في الذِّهْنِ أوْ في الخارِجِ، مِن كَوْنِها مَظْنُونَةً أوْ مُتَيَقِّنَةً، فَتَقْتَضِي مَفْعُولَيْنِ أصْلُهُما المُبْتَدَأُ والخَبَرُ أوْ ما يَسُدُّ مَسَدَّهُما، وقَدْ سَدَّ مَسَدَّهُما هُنا عَلى ما قالَهُ الحَوْفِيُّ وابْنُ عَطِيَّةَ وأبُو البَقاءِ: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾. وسَدَّ ﴿أنِ﴾ المَصْدَرِيَّةُ النّاصِبَةُ لِلْفِعْلِ (أنِ المصدرية الناصبة: الحرف الذي يجعل الفعل المضارع بعده مؤولًا بمصدر ويُنصب) مَعَ مَدْخُولِها مَسَدَّ الجُزْأيْنِ، مِمّا قالَهُ ابْنُ مالِكٍ، ونَقَلَهُ عَنْهُ الدَّمامِينِيُّ في شَرْحِ التَّسْهِيلِ، وزَعَمَ بَعْضُهم أنَّ ذَلِكَ إنَّما هو في ﴿أنَّ﴾ المَفْتُوحَةِ مُشَدَّدَةً ومُثَقَّلَةً مَعَ مَدْخُولِها، والتَّرْكُ هُنا عَلى ما ذَكَرَهُ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ بِمَعْنى التَّصْيِيرِ المُتَعَدِّي لِمَفْعُولَيْنِ، كَما في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وتَرَكَهم في ظُلُماتٍ لا يُبْصِرُونَ﴾ [البَقَرَةِ: 17]، وقَوْلِ الشّاعِرِ:

فَتَرَكَتْهُ جُزُرُ السِّباعِ يَنُشُّنَّهُ يَقْضِمْنَ قِلَّةَ رَأْسِهِ والمِعْصَمِ

فَضَمِيرُ الجَمْعِ نائِبُ مَفْعُولٍ أوَّلَ، والمَفْعُولُ الثّانِي مَتْرُوكٌ بِدَلالَةِ الحالِ الآتِيَةِ، أيْ: كَما هم، أوْ عَلى ما هم عَلَيْهِ، كَما في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿أمْ حَسِبْتُمْ أنْ تُتْرَكُوا ولَمّا يَعْلَمِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ جاهَدُوا مِنكم ولَمْ يَتَّخِذُوا﴾ [التَّوْبَةِ: 16]، عَلى ما قَدَّرَهُ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ فِيهِ. وقَوْلُهُ سُبْحانَهُ: ﴿أنْ يَقُولُوا آمَنّا﴾ بِمَعْنى ﴿لِأنْ يَقُولُوا﴾ مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِـ﴿يَتْرُكُوا﴾ عَلى أنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُسْتَقِرٍّ. وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وهم لا يُفْتَنُونَ﴾ في مَوْضِعِ الحالِ مِن ضَمِيرِ ﴿يَتْرُكُوا﴾. ويَجُوزُ أنْ لا يُعْتَبَرَ كَوْنُ المَفْعُولِ الثّانِي لِـ﴿يَتْرُكُوا﴾ مَتْرُوكًا، بَلْ تُجْعَلُ هَذِهِ الجُمْلَةُ الحالِيَّةُ سادَّةً مَسَدَّهُ، أَلا تَرى أنَّكَ لَوْ قُلْتَ: عَلِمْتُ ضَرْبِي زَيْدًا قائِمًا صَحَّ؟ عَلى أنَّ تَرْكَ لَيْسَ كَأفْعالِ القُلُوبِ في جَمِيعِ الأحْكامِ، بَلِ القِياسُ أنْ يَجُوزَ الِاكْتِفاءُ فِيهِ بِالحالِ مِن غَيْرِ نَظَرٍ إلى أنَّهُ قائِمٌ مَقامَ الثّانِي، لِأنَّ قَوْلَكَ: تَرَكَتْهُ وهو جَزْرَ السِّباعِ، كَلامٌ صَحِيحٌ، كَما تَقُولُ: أبْقَيْتُهُ عَلى هَذِهِ الحالَةِ، وهو نَظِيرُ: سَمِعْتُهُ يَتَحَدَّثُ، في أنَّهُ يَتِمُّ بِالحالِ بَعْدَهُ أوِ الوَصْفِ، وهاهُنا زادَ أنَّهُ يَتِمُّ أيْضًا بِما يَجْرِي مَجْرى الخَبَرِ. وجُوِّزَ أنْ تَكُونَ هَذِهِ الجُمْلَةُ هي المَفْعُولَ الثّانِيَ لا سادَّةً مَسَدَّهُ، وتَوَسُّطُ الواوِ بَيْنَ المَفْعُولَيْنِ جائِزٌ، كَما في قَوْلِهِ:

وصَيَّرَنِي هَواكِ وبِي ∗∗∗ لِحِينِي يُضْرَبُ المَثَلُ

وقَدْ نَصَّ شارِحُ أبْياتِ المُفَصَّلِ عَلى أنَّهُ حُكِيَ عَنِ الأخْفَشِ أنَّهُ كانَ يَجُوزُ: كانَ زَيْدٌ وأبُوهُ قائِمٌ، عَلى نُقْصانِ كانَ، وجَعْلِ الجُمْلَةِ خَبَرًا مَعَ الواوِ تَشْبِيهًا لِخَبَرِ كانَ بِالحالِ، فَمَتى جازَ في الخَبَرِ عِنْدَهُ فَلْيَجُزْ في المَفْعُولِ الثّانِي، وهو كَما نَرى. واسْتَظْهَرَ الطَّيِّبِيُّ كَوْنَ التَّرْكِ هُنا مُتَعَدِّيًا لِواحِدٍ عَلى أنَّهُ بِمَعْنى التَّخْلِيَةِ، ولَيْسَ بِذاكَ. وجَوَّزَ الحَوْفِيُّ وأبُو البَقاءِ أنْ يَكُونَ ﴿أنْ يَقُولُوا﴾ بَدَلًا مِن ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾. وجُوِّزَ أنْ يَكُونَ ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾ هو المَفْعُولَ الأوَّلَ لِـ﴿حَسِبَ﴾، و﴿وهم لا يُفْتَنُونَ﴾ في مَوْضِعِ الحالِ مِنَ الضَّمِيرِ، و﴿أنْ يَقُولُوا﴾ بِتَقْدِيرِ اللّامِ هو المَفْعُولُ الثّانِي، وكَوْنُهُ عِلَّةً لا يُنافِي ذَلِكَ، كَما في قَوْلِكَ: حَسِبْتُ ضَرْبَهُ لِلتَّأْدِيبِ، والتَّقْدِيرُ: أحَسِبَ النّاسُ تَرْكَهم غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ لِقَوْلِهِمْ: آمَنّا، والمَفْعُولُ الثّانِي لِـ﴿يُتْرَكُوا﴾ مَتْرُوكٌ بِدَلالَةِ الحالِ. واعْتَرَضَهُ صاحِبُ التَّقْرِيبِ بِما حاصِلُهُ: أنَّ الحُسْبانَ لِتَعَلُّقِهِ بِمَضامِينِ الجُمَلِ، إذا أُنْكِرَ يَكُونُ بِاعْتِبارِ المَفْعُولِ الثّانِي، فَإذا قُلْتَ: أحَسِبْتَهُ قائِمًا؟ فالمُنْكَرُ حُسْبانُ قِيامِهِ، وكَذَلِكَ إذا قِيلَ: أحَسِبَ النّاسُ تَرْكَهم غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ لِقَوْلِهِمْ آمَنّا، أفادَ إنْكارَ حُسْبانِ أنَّ التَّرْكَ غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ لِهَذِهِ العِلَّةِ، بَلْ إنَّما هو لِعِلَّةٍ أُخْرى، ولا يُلائِمُ سَبَبَ النُّزُولِ ولا مَقْصُودَ الآيَةِ.

واخْتارَ أنْ يَكُونَ ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾ سادًّا مَسَدَّ المَفْعُولَيْنِ، و﴿أنْ يَقُولُوا﴾ عِلَّةٌ لِلْحُسْبانِ، أيْ: أحَسِبُوا لِقَوْلِهِمْ آمَنّا
صفحة 134
أنْ يُتْرَكُوا غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ؟ وأُجِيبُ بِأنَّ أصْلَ الكَلامِ: ألّا يُفْتَنُوا لِقَوْلِهِمْ آمَنّا، عَلى إنْكارِ أنْ يَكُونَ سَبَبًا لِعَدَمِ الفِتَنِ، ثُمَّ قِيلَ:

أيُتْرَكُونَ غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ لِقَوْلِهِمْ آمَنّا؟ مُبالَغَةً في إنْكارِ أنْ يَبْقَوْا مِن غَيْرِ فِتَنٍ لِذَلِكَ، ثُمَّ أدْخَلَ عَلى حُسْبانِ التَّرْكِ مُبالَغَةً عَلى مُبالَغَةٍ. وإنَّما يُرَدُّ ما أُورِدَ إذا لَمْ يُلاحَظْ أصْلُ الكَلامِ، ويُجْعَلْ مَصَبُّ الإنْكارِ الحُسْبانَ مِن أوَّلِ الأمْرِ.

وقِيلَ: إنَّما يَلْزَمُ ما ذُكِرَ لَوْ لَمْ يُقَدَّرْ: أحَسِبُوا تَرْكَهم غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ بِمُجَرَّدِ قَوْلِهِمْ: آمَنّا، دُونَ إخْلاصٍ وعَمَلٍ صالِحٍ؛ أمّا لَوْ قُدِّرَ ذَلِكَ اسْتَقامَ، كَما صَرَّحَ بِهِ الزَّجّاجُ، عَلى أنَّ ذَلِكَ مَبْنِيٌّ عَلى اعْتِبارِ المَفْهُومِ. واعْتَرَضَ ذَلِكَ بَعْضُهم مِن حَيْثُ اللَّفْظُ بِأنَّ فِيهِ الفَصْلَ بَيْنَ الحالِ وذِيها بِثانِي مَفْعُولَيْ ﴿حَسِبَ﴾، وهو أجْنَبِيٌّ. وأُجِيبُ بِأنَّ الفَصْلَ غَيْرُ مُمْتَنِعٍ، بَلِ الأحْسَنُ أنْ لا يَقَعَ فَصْلٌ إلّا إذا اعْتَرَضَ ما يُوجِبُهُ، وهاهُنا الِاهْتِمامُ بِشَأْنِ الخَبَرِ حَسَنُ التَّقْدِيمِ، لِأنَّ مَصَبَّ الإنْكارِ ذَلِكَ. ولا يَخْفى أنَّهُ يَحْتاجُ إلى مِثْلِ هَذا الجَوابِ عَلى ما يَقْتَضِيهِ الظّاهِرُ مِن جَعْلِ ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾ في تَأْوِيلِ مَصْدَرٍ وقَعَ مَفْعُولًا أوَّلًا، و﴿أنْ يَقُولُوا﴾ في تَأْوِيلِ مَصْدَرٍ أيْضًا مَجْرُورٍ بِلامٍ مُقَدَّرَةٍ، والجارُّ والمَجْرُورُ في مَوْقِعِ المَفْعُولِ الثّانِي. وأمّا عَلى ما ذَكَرَهُ بَعْضُ المُحَقِّقِينَ، مِن أنَّهُما لَمْ يُجْعَلا كَذَلِكَ، وإنَّما جُعِلَ ﴿أنْ يَقُولُوا﴾ مَعْمُولًا لِـ﴿يَتْرُكُوا﴾ بِتَقْدِيرِ اللّامِ، وجُعِلَ ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾ سادًّا مَسَدَّ المَفْعُولَيْنِ، واقْتَضى المَعْنى أنْ يُقالَ: أحَسِبَ النّاسُ تَرْكَهم غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ لِقَوْلِهِمْ آمَنّا، بِجَعْلِ تَرْكِهِمْ مَفْعُولًا أوَّلًا، ولِقَوْلِهِمْ مَفْعُولًا ثانِيًا، فَلا يُحْتاجُ إلَيْهِ؛ لِأنَّهُ إنْ جَرَيْنا مَعَ اللَّفْظِ كانَ ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾ سادًّا مَسَدَّ المَفْعُولَيْنِ، فَلا يَكُونُ فِيهِ مَفْعُولٌ ثانٍ فاصِلٌ بَيْنَ الحالِ وذِيها، وإنْ جَرَيْنا مَعَ المَعْنى، واعْتَبَرْنا الكَلامَ مُجَرَّدًا عَنْ ﴿أنِ﴾ المَصْدَرِيَّةِ، وجِيءَ بِهِ كَما سَمِعْتَ، كانَتِ الحالُ مُتَّصِلَةً بِذِيها. وقِيلَ: يَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ المَفْعُولُ الأوَّلُ لِـ﴿حَسِبَ﴾ مَحْذُوفًا، أيْ: أحَسِبَ النّاسُ أنْفُسَهم، و﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾ في مَوْضِعِ المَفْعُولِ الثّانِي عَلى أنَّهُ في تَأْوِيلِ مَصْدَرٍ، وهو في تَأْوِيلِ اسْمِ المَفْعُولِ، أيْ: مَتْرُوكِينَ، و﴿وهم لا يُفْتَنُونَ﴾ في مَوْضِعِ الحالِ كَما تَقَدَّمَ، و﴿أنْ يُؤْمِنُوا﴾ بِتَقْدِيرِ ﴿لِأنْ يُؤْمِنُوا﴾ مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِـ﴿يُتْرَكُوا﴾، فَكَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: أحَسِبَ النّاسُ أنْفُسَهم مَتْرُوكِينَ غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ لِقَوْلِهِمْ آمَنّا. وقِيلَ: إنَّ هَذا المَعْنى حاصِلٌ عَلى تَقْدِيرِ سَدِّ ﴿أنْ يُتْرَكُوا﴾ مَسَدَّ المَفْعُولَيْنِ، فَتَأمَّلْ فِيهِ وفِيما قَبْلَهُ. ولَعَلَّ الأبْعَدَ عَنِ التَّكَلُّفِ ما ذَكَرْناهُ أوَّلًا، والمُرادُ: إنْكارُ حُسْبانِهِمْ أنْ يُتْرَكُوا غَيْرَ مَفْتُونِينَ بِمُجَرَّدِ أنْ يَقُولُوا آمَنّا، واسْتِبْعادٌ لَهُ، وتَحْقِيقُ أنَّهُ تَعالى يَمْتَحِنُهم بِمَشاقِّ التَّكالِيفِ، كَالمُهاجَرَةِ والمُجاهَدَةِ، ورَفْضِ الشَّهَواتِ، ووَظائِفِ الطّاعاتِ، وفُنُونِ المَصائِبِ في الأنْفُسِ والأمْوالِ، لِيَتَمَيَّزَ المُخْلِصُ مِنَ المُنافِقِ، والرّاسِخُ في الدِّينِ مِنَ المُتَزَلْزِلِ فِيهِ، فَيُعامَلُ كُلٌّ بِما يَقْتَضِيهِ، ويُجازِيهِمْ سُبْحانَهُ بِحَسَبِ مَراتِبِ أعْمالِهِمْ، فَإنَّ مُجَرَّدَ الإيمانِ وإنْ كانَ عَنْ خُلُوصٍ، لا يَقْتَضِي غَيْرَ الخَلاصِ مِنَ الخُلُودِ في النّارِ.

وذَكَرَ بَعْضُهم أنَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ لَوْ أثابَ المُؤْمِنَ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ مِن غَيْرِ أنْ يَفْتِنَهُ في الدُّنْيا، لَقالَ الكافِرُ المُعَذَّبُ: رَبِّي، لَوْ أنَّكَ كُنْتَ فَتَنْتَهُ في الدُّنْيا لَكَفَرَ مِثْلِي! فَإيمانُهُ الَّذِي تُثِيبُهُ عَلَيْهِ مِمّا لا يَسْتَحِقُّ الثَّوابَ لَهُ، فَبِالفِتْنَةِ يُلْجَمُ الكافِرُ عَنْ مِثْلِ هَذا القَوْلِ، ويُعَوَّضُ المُؤْمِنُ بَدَلَها ما يُعَوَّضُ، بِحَيْثُ يَتَمَنّى لَوْ كانَتْ فِتْنَتُهُ أعْظَمَ مِمّا كانَتْ. والآيَةُ عَلى ما أخْرَجَ عَبْدُ بْنُ حُمَيْدٍ وابْنُ جَرِيرٍ وابْنُ المُنْذِرِ وابْنُ أبِي حاتِمٍ عَنِ الشَّعْبِيِّ: نَزَلَتْ في أُناسٍ كانُوا بِمَكَّةَ قَدْ أقَرُّوا بِالإسْلامِ، فَكَتَبَ إلَيْهِمْ أصْحابُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) مِنَ المَدِينَةِ، لَمّا نَزَلَتْ آيَةُ الهِجْرَةِ: أنَّهُ لا يُقْبَلُ مِنكم إقْرارٌ ولا إسْلامٌ حَتّى تُهاجِرُوا، فَخَرَجُوا عامِدِينَ إلى المَدِينَةِ، فاتَّبَعَهُمُ المُشْرِكُونَ فَرَدُّوهم، فَنَزَلَتْ فِيهِمْ هَذِهِ الآيَةُ، فَكَتَبُوا إلَيْهِمْ: أنْزَلَتْ فِيكم آيَةُ كَذا وكَذا؟ فَقالُوا: نَخْرُجُ، فَإنِ اتَّبَعَنا أحَدٌ قاتَلْناهُ، فَخَرَجُوا فاتَّبَعَهُمُ المُشْرِكُونَ فَقاتَلُوهم

فَمِنهم مَن قُتِلَ ومِنهم مَن نَجا، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ تَعالى فِيهِمْ: ﴿ثُمَّ إنَّ رَبَّكَ لِلَّذِينَ هاجَرُوا مِن بَعْدِ ما فُتِنُوا ثُمَّ جاهَدُوا وصَبَرُوا إنَّ رَبَّكَ مِن بَعْدِها لَغَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ [النَّحْلِ: 110].

وأخْرَجَ ابْنُ المُنْذِرِ عَنِ ابْنِ جُرَيْجٍ قالَ: سَمِعْتُ ابْنَ عُمَيْرٍ وغَيْرَهُ يَقُولُونَ: كانَ أبُو جَهْلٍ يُعَذِّبُ عَمّارَ بْنَ ياسِرٍ وأُمَّهُ، ويَجْعَلُ عَلى عَمّارٍ دِرْعًا مِن حَدِيدٍ في اليَوْمِ الصّائِفِ، وطَعَنَ في فَرْجِ أُمِّهِ بِرُمْحٍ، فَفي ذَلِكَ نَزَلَتْ: ﴿أحَسِبَ النّاسُ﴾ إلَخْ. وقِيلَ: نَزَلَتْ في مَهْجَعٍ مَوْلى عُمَرَ بْنِ الخَطّابِ، قُتِلَ بِبَدْرٍ، فَجَزِعَ عَلَيْهِ أبَواهُ وامْرَأتُهُ، «وقالَ فِيهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ (ﷺ): سَيِّدُ الشُّهَداءِ مَهْجَعٌ، وهو أوَّلُ مَن يُدْعى إلى بابِ الجَنَّةِ». وقِيلَ: نَزَلَتْ في عَيّاشٍ أخِي أبِي جَهْلٍ، غَدَرَ وعَذَّبَ لِيَرْتَدَّ، كَما سَيَأْتِي خَبَرُهُ إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ تَعالى. وفُسِّرَ "النّاسُ" بِمَن نَزَلَتْ فِيهِمُ الآيَةُ، وقالَ الحَسَنُ: النّاسُ هُنا المُنافِقُونَ.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 3:

﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from "the people" or from the pronoun in "they will be tested." On the first view, it is a reason for the denial of the supposition: "Do they think that [this], while they know that the way (sunnah) of Allah the Exalted is contrary to it? And you will never find any change in the way of Allah the Exalted." On the second view, it is an explanation, since there is no basis for singling them out as exempt from being tested. The upshot is that on the first view it is an admonition about the error, and on the second it is a rebuke. What is meant by "those before them" are the believers, the followers of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, who suffered every kind of trial and tribulation that befell them; so they endured and clung to their religion with their molars, as is indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And how many a prophet has fought, with him many devoted followers. They did not weaken for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they become weak or submit﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146], and so on. Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i related from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who said: "We complained to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, and we had indeed suffered severe hardship from the polytheists. We said: 'Will you not seek help for us? Will you not supplicate for us?' He said: 'Among those before you, a man would be seized, a pit dug for him in the earth, and he would be placed in it. Then a saw would be brought and placed on his head, and he would be split in two. And iron combs would be run over him, tearing the flesh and bone from his body, yet that would not turn him from his religion.'"

﴿So Allah will certainly know those who are truthful﴾, that is, in their saying "We believe," ﴿and He will certainly know the liars﴾ in that. The "fa" (so) indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, which makes clear the occurrence of the test. The "lam" is in the answer to the oath. The shift to the name "Allah" serves to instil awe and to cultivate reverence, and the repetition of the answer serves to add emphasis and affirmation. It may be imagined from the verse that His knowledge, exalted be He, comes into being with the occurrences, and this is false. It is answered that the knowledge of Allah the Exalted relates to the thing after it has come into being, as a non-existent. Ibn al-Munir said: The truth is that the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is one; it relates to the existent at the time of its existence, before it and after it, as it is. The benefit of mentioning knowledge here, although it precedes the existence of the thing known, is to alert, by the cause, to the effect, which is the recompense. It is as if it were said: "By Allah, He will surely know, through what resembles a trial and testing, those who were truthful in the faith they manifested, and those who are liars in it, persisting in lying; so He will surely requite each according to what He knows of him." Its meaning is also what Ibn Jinni said, that it is the placing of the cause in the position of the effect, and the purpose is: "Allah the Exalted will surely reward those who were truthful, and will surely requite the liars," because reward for a thing is only caused by knowledge. Muhyi al-Sunnah said: That is, Allah the Exalted will make manifest the truthful from the liars, so that it is found known, because Allah the Exalted knows them before the testing.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad and al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with them, read "falayu'limanna" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the lām.

It is the imperfect of a'lama, formed with the causative hamza from 'alima, which is transitive to one object and means "to know" in the sense of "to recognize." On this reading the verb is transitive to two objects, and the second is omitted here: "So Allah will surely make known to those who were truthful their stations of reward, and the liars their stations of punishment," and that is in the Hereafter. Or the first object is omitted: "So Allah will surely make the people know those who were truthful, and He will surely make the liars know them," that is, He will show these in good and those in evil. The apparent meaning is that this too is in the Hereafter. Abu Hayyan said: in this world and the Hereafter. It is also permitted that this be from "i'lam," which is the placing of a mark or sign, and then it is transitive to one object, meaning He will mark them with a sign by which they are recognized on the Day of Resurrection, such as the whiteness and blackness of faces. It was also said: He, glory be to Him, will mark them with a sign by which they are recognized in this world.

As in His statement, upon him be blessings and peace: "Whoever conceals an inner intention, Allah the Exalted will clothe him in its mantle."

Al-Zuhri read the first verb as the others read it, and the second verb as Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ja'far and al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with them, read it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 4:

﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they can outrun Us?﴾ Mujahid said: That is, they will render Us powerless, so that We cannot requite them for their deeds or take vengeance upon them. The root of sabq (outrunning) is escape (fawt), and then it was intended in the sense mentioned. It was also said: that is, they will hasten Us toward the decreed, inevitable judgment. The first (interpretation) is preferable.

Qatada interpreted "evil deeds" (al-sayyi'at) as shirk (polytheism), as related by Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir from him. The plural is used in view of the multiplicity of those who are characterized by it, and "deed" is applied to shirk, whether we say it is what is done without thought and deliberation, as has been said, or what is done intentionally, as al-Raghib said, or not; there is no harm in it, since it occurs through the worship of idols and other things. It was also said: the intended meaning of "evil deeds" is sins other than disbelief, so the verse is definitely about believers. Although they did not think that they could escape Him, the Exalted, and their souls did not yearn for that, nevertheless their persistence was treated, through their heedlessness and their insistence upon sins, as the state of one who is not certain of the recompense and who thinks that he can escape Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Some scholars generalised and took "evil deeds" to mean both disbelief and sins. Attaching the action to them, on the premise that the restriction to what you have heard is accepted, may be understood as a case of taghlib (predominance of one term over another). The apparent sense of the reports indicates that this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: By "those who commit evil deeds" He, glorified be He, means al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-Aswad, al-As ibn Hisham, Shayba, Utba, al-Walid ibn Utba, Utba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, Hanzala ibn Wa'il, and their likes among the chieftains of Quraysh. In al-Bahr it is stated that although the verse was revealed on a specific occasion, it encompasses all who commit evil deeds, both disbeliever and Muslim. The apparent view is that "am" (or) is disjunctive (munqati'a), in the sense of bal (rather), which is used for transition, and this is a transition from denying the supposition that the absence of trials is due merely to faith, to denying the supposition that there is no requital for committing evil deeds.

Ibn Atiyya said: "am" is equivalent to the hamza in His statement, Exalted be He: ﴿Do they think...﴾, as if He, glorified be He, established both groups: He established the believers in their assumption that they would not be tested, and He established the disbelievers who commit evil deeds, by harming the believers and otherwise, in their assumption that they would outrun the retributions of Allah, Exalted be He, and render Him powerless. End of quote. It was refuted: if it were equivalent to the hamza, it would be connected (muttasila), and the consequent is false, because the condition for a connected "am" is that what follows it be a single term, such as "Is Zayd standing or Amr?", or what is equivalent to a single term, such as "Did Zayd stand or sit?", and its answer is the specification of one of the two things or of several things. Here what follows it is a clause, and it is impossible to answer here with one of the two things either. Therefore the correct view is that it is disjunctive, and the interrogation that it implies is one of denial, which does not require an answer, as is not hidden. The apparent view is that the verb hasiba (to think) is transitive to two objects, and that "an yasbiquna-na" (that they outrun Us) fills the place of both.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted here that it should be taken to imply the meaning of thinking (taqdir), so that it is transitive to one object, and that "an yasbiquna-na" is that one object.

Abu Hayyan criticised him, saying that implication (tadmin) is not a regular rule and is resorted to only when needed, and here there is no need for it.

﴿Evil is what they judge﴾: that is, wretched is the judgment they make. On this reading, sa'a means bi'sa, and ma is a relative pronoun, with "yahkumun" as its relative clause, the returning pronoun being omitted; it is the subject of sa'a, and the object of blame is omitted. Or: wretched is the judgment they make, on the reading that ma is a descriptive (maws'uf) noun, "yahkumun" is its descriptor, the connecting pronoun is omitted, it is a specifying term (tamyiz), the subject of sa'a is a pronoun explained by the specifying term, and the object of blame is likewise omitted.

Ibn Kaysan said: ma is verbal-noun (masdariyya), and the resulting verbal phrase is the object of blame, so the specifying term is omitted. It was also permitted that sa'a means qabuha (was ugly), and ma is either masdariyya, relative, or descriptive. The present tense indicates continuity, a sign that this is their habit, or it stands in place of the past for the sake of the fasila (verse-ending rhyme). Both of these views are related by al-Bahr, and the first is preferable. In my opinion, such a construction is used only with regard to...

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "The meaning is: whoever fears being resurrected in the Hereafter. Here *al-raja'* (hope) means *al-khawf* (fear), as in the words of al-Hudhali describing a honey-collector:

*When the stinging insects sting him, he does not expect their sting, and he goes against them into the hives of the working bees.*

It is likely that what is meant by meeting Him, Mighty and Majestic, is the resurrection, since it is among its beginnings. It has also been said that he used the meeting with God, exalted is He, as an expression for arriving at the outcome, but since the resurrection is among the greatest things on which that depends, he singled it out for mention. In *al-Kashshaf* it is stated that the meeting with God, exalted is He, is a *mathal* (parable, a figurative illustration) for arriving at the outcome, through receiving the Angel of Death, the resurrection, the reckoning and the recompense. That state is depicted by the state of a servant who comes before his master after a long absence, while his master has become aware of what he used to do and leave undone. Then either the master meets him with cheerfulness and welcome, because of what he approved of his deeds, or with the opposite, because of what he disliked of them. So the meaning of ﴿whoever used to﴾ etc. is: whoever used to hope for that state and to meet therein honour from God and glad tidings. According to him, the statement is by way of *tamthil* (parable), and *al-raja'* means hope and expectation.

It is permissible that it means the same, except that the statement contains an elided *mudaf* (an omitted noun in a genitive construction), meaning: whoever used to expect the meeting of God's recompense, reward or punishment, or the meeting of His judgment on the Day of Resurrection. It is also permissible that it means fear, with the *mudaf* likewise omitted, meaning: whoever used to fear the meeting of God's punishment. It is also permissible that it means the supposition that what is pleasing will occur and the expectation of it, as is well known, with the *mudaf* likewise omitted, meaning: whoever used to hope for the meeting of God's reward. It is also permissible that no *mudaf* is supposed, and that the meeting with God, exalted is He, be taken as a *majaz* (figurative usage) for the reward, because it is necessarily connected to it.

Some have chosen that *al-raja'* has its well-known meaning, and that the meeting with God, exalted is He, is the beholding of Him, glorified is He, in the manner fitting to Him, Mighty and Majestic, as the People of the Sunnah and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah*) say, since there is no need to depart from the apparent meaning without necessity. What the Mu'tazili supposed of it is not part of it, as is explained in *'ilm al-kalam* (theological discourse). That is: whoever used to expect the beholding of God, exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection, which no bliss equals and which entails success in every good and bliss. ﴿Then surely the term of God﴾: *al-ajal* is the end point of an extended period of time designated for a matter among matters, and it may also be applied to that whole period of time, though the first usage is more common. That is: the time He, glorified is His affair, has appointed for that ﴿is surely coming﴾ without doubt, with no diverter to turn it aside and no restrainer to hold it back, because the parts of time are constantly passing away and ending. The coming of that time is a *kinayah* (metonymy) for the arrival of what is in it and its occurrence. The nominal sentence stands in the place of the answer to the conditional, and in reality it is the indicator of the elided answer, meaning: let him hasten to do what brings him closer to compliance with the commands and avoidance of the prohibitions, or let him hasten to do what fulfils his hope and makes his expectation true, or something similar that fits the condition. So reflect.

It has been said: it is permissible that the nominal sentence itself be the answer, on the basis that what is meant by it is the meaning suited to the condition, as has been mentioned. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾, exalted is His majesty, of the words of His servants, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of their states, both their outward deeds and their beliefs and inward attributes. The sentence is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) to confirm the realisation of what is hoped for and what is feared, as promise and as threat.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 6:

﴿And whoever strives﴾ in obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿then he strives only for himself﴾, because the benefit of the reward prepared for that returns to him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾. So He has no need of their obedience, and He commanded them to it, may He be glorified, only to expose them to the reward, in accordance with His mercy and wisdom.

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾: the disbelief, whether original or acquired, is removed by faith, and the sins are removed by the acts of obedience that follow them. ﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾, meaning the best reward for their deeds. A good reward is that a good deed be rewarded with a good deed, and the best reward is that one good deed be rewarded with ten and more. It has been said that if it is taken as "We will surely reward them with the best of their deeds" or "the reward for the best of their deeds," this allows the exclusion of the permissible (mubah).

﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾, meaning We commanded him to attend to them and to honour them. The word ḥusnan (kindness) is in the accusative because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning "an enjoining, good," that is, "possessing goodness," or it is itself good because of its extreme goodness, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And speak to people kindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. This is what Abu Hayyan preferred, and it is not free of good. Al-Zamakhshari said: ḥasanan is a direct object (maf'ul bihi) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar) that is annexed to "his parents," meaning "We enjoined him to give his parents [their due] or to show his parents kindness." In this there is the government (i'mal) of an omitted masdar while retaining its governing power, which is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra). It is also permitted that ḥusnan be a masdar of an omitted verb, meaning "he did well, a goodness," and the clause is in the place of the object of waṣṣā (enjoined), because it contains the meaning of saying. This is according to the view of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa), who hold that what contains the meaning of saying may govern clauses without an implied verb of saying. According to the Basrans, a verb of saying is implied in such cases, and on that basis it is permitted that it be a direct object of an omitted verb, with the clause being the content of the saying, and the clause of saying explaining the enjoining, meaning "We said, the first of them," or "Do good to the two of them." On this basis it is good to pause at "to his parents," because the following clause begins a new sentence. He preferred the implied imperative because it is more suited to what follows of direct address and prohibition, which is its counterpart, but he weakened the view that involves many implied elements by the abundance of implication. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah related from the Kufans that they make ḥusnan a direct object of an omitted verb and imply that he "should do kindness," and in this there is the omission of anna (that) and its clause while the governed noun remains, which is not permitted according to the Basrans. It has also been said that ḥusnan is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, and that "to his parents" is connected to waṣṣainā (We enjoined), with the bāʾ meaning fī (in), meaning "We enjoined man concerning the matter of his parents with goodness." This, as you see, is [weak].

ʿĪsā and al-Jaḥdarī read ḥasanan with two fatḥas (vowels). In the codex of Ubayy it is iḥsānan (kindness).

﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them﴾: this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what precedes it, and the verb of saying must be implied if it was not implied earlier, meaning "And We said: If they strive with you," and so on, so that the coordination of performative speech (inshaʾ) with declarative speech (khabar) does not occur. The conditional clause, when its response is performative, is itself performative, as they have stated. So if the verb of saying is not implied, it is not fitting to coordinate it with "We enjoined," for the reason mentioned, nor with what governs it, because it has the meaning of saying, and that is better. Even if the two agree in being performative, it is not part of the enjoining concerning parents, because it forbids obeying them. As for its coordination with "We said," which explains the enjoining, there is no harm in it, because the enjoining is thereby restricted by not leading ultimately to disobedience. It is as if it were said: "Be kind to them and obey them as long as they do not command you to disobedience." So reflect.

The apparent meaning required by the context is that mā (what) is general, covering everything other than Him, exalted is His majesty. His saying, glorified is He, "of which (bihi)," is by the omission of a modifier, meaning "of whose divinity you have no knowledge." The indefiniteness of ʿilm (knowledge) is for belittling it.

What is meant by "to make you associate with Me" is something that cannot be a god and that cannot be correct. In the turning away from it to the wording of the sublime text there is an announcement [p. 139] that what is not known to be sound, even in general terms, as in blind imitation (taqlid), may not be followed, even if its falsity is not known, so how much more so what is known in the most complete way to be false. The scholar al-Ṭībī took the negation of knowledge as a metonymy (kinayah) for the negation of the known, and he justified this by saying that this style is commonly used regarding God, exalted is He, such as "Do you inform God of what He does not know?" Then he said: In it there is an indication that the negation of associating partners belongs to the necessary knowledge, and that the sound natural disposition (fitrah) is innately inclined to it, according to what is reported: "Every child is born upon the fitrah."

That is because the one addressed by His saying, exalted is He:

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 29, verse 8:

﴿And We have enjoined upon man﴾: "man" here refers to the human species in general, end of quote. There is a point of discussion here. The object of "do not obey them" (lā tuṭi'humā) is omitted, because the meaning of the statement makes it clear. The implied sense is: "Even if they exert their utmost effort to make you associate with Me others that have no divinity, do not obey them in that, for there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator." In making the prohibition against obeying them conditional upon their striving to make you comply, there is an indication that the reason for the prohibition applies a fortiori to lesser demands, and likewise its reason applies to striving by either of them.

﴿To Me is your return﴾: that is, the return of whoever among you believed, whoever associated partners with Allah, whoever was dutiful, and whoever was disobedient. This sentence confirms what precedes it, and for this reason it is not joined by a conjunction (ʿaṭf).

﴿Then I will inform you of what you used to do﴾: by recompensing each of you for his deed, so that if it is good, the reward is good, and if it is evil, the recompense is evil.

It is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him. When he embraced Islam, his mother Hamnah bint Abi Sufyan ibn Umayyah ibn ʿAbd Shams said: "O Saʿd, I have heard that you have turned away (ṣabaʾta). By Allah, the roof of a house will not shade me from the sun's heat (ḍiḥḥ) and the wind, and food and drink are forbidden to me (ʿalayya) until you disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ)." She was the dearest of her children to her. Saʿd refused, and she remained like that for three days. Then Saʿd came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained to him. So this verse was revealed, along with the one in Luqman and the one in al-Ahqaf. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then commanded him to be patient with her (yudārīhā) and to win her good pleasure (yatarāḍāhā) through kindness.

It is also narrated that it was revealed concerning ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah al-Makhzumi. He had emigrated together with ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as they were in agreement, until they both reached Medina. Then Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and al-Harith ibn Hisham, his two maternal brothers, the sons of Asma bint Makhramah, a woman of the Banu Tamim, of the Banu Handhalah, went out and came to ʿAyyash and said to him: "Muhammad's religion includes maintaining the ties of kinship and being dutiful to parents. You have left your mother, who will not eat, drink, or take shelter under any roof until she sees you, and she loves you more than we do. So come out with us." They kept at him, and he was swayed by them at the top and back of his mind (fatlan minhu fi al-dhurwa wa al-gharib). He consulted ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "They are deceiving you. But for me, I will divide my wealth between myself and you." They kept at him until he obeyed her and disobeyed ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him. Then ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Since you have disobeyed me, take my camel, for there is no camel in the world that can catch up with her. If you have any doubt about them, return." When they reached the desert (al-bayda'), Abu Jahl said: "My camel has become exhausted, so carry me with you." He said: "Yes." So he (ʿAyyash) made his camel kneel for him (to mount).

Then they seized him, tied him up, and each of them lashed him one hundred times, and they took him back to his mother. She said: "You will not cease to be in torment until you turn away from the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ)." Then the verse was revealed.

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds – We will surely admit them among the righteous.﴾ That is, into the company of those firmly established in righteousness (*ṣalāḥ*), perfect in it. *Ṣalāḥ* is the opposite of corruption (*fasād*), and it encompasses every good. It has countless degrees, and the degree of perfection in it is a lofty one. For this reason the prophets, peace be upon them, sought it, as Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [an-Naml: 19].

It is possible that the speech is by way of an elided genitive (*taqdīr muḍāf*), meaning "into the abode of the righteous," which is Paradise. In that case the relative pronoun *alladhīna* is the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the sentence), and *la-nudkhilannahum* is the predicate (*khabar*), according to what Abu al-Baqa' mentioned. It is also permitted that *alladhīna* be in the position of an accusative, under the assumption of *la-nudkhilanna alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt la-nudkhilannahum* (the verb being repeated in the first clause).

[Page 140]

﴿And among the people﴾, i.e., some of them, ﴿are those who say, "We believe in Allah," but when they are harmed for the sake of Allah﴾, i.e., for His sake, mighty and majestic is He, with "fi" here indicating causation; or the meaning is "in the way of Allah, the Exalted," that the polytheists tortured them for their faith in Him, exalted is He, ﴿they regard the trial inflicted by people﴾, i.e., they treat what afflicts them from their harm as ﴿like the punishment of Allah﴾, i.e., as equal to His punishment in the Hereafter. So they panic at that, do not endure it, obey the people, and disbelieve in Allah, exalted is He, just as one obeys Allah, exalted is He, when one fears His punishment, glorified is He, and so believes in Him, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And if a victory comes from your Lord﴾, namely that the believers gain a conquest and spoils, ﴿they will surely say﴾ (with the second lam pronounced with a damma, and the plural pronoun omitted because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters; this pronoun refers back to "man," and the plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular pronouns referring to it earlier are used in view of its wording). Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi reported that it was read as "layaqulanna" with a fatha on the lam, using the singular pronoun as in what preceded. ﴿"Indeed we were with you"﴾, i.e., supporting you in the religion, so include us in the spoils that were obtained. It was also said: i.e., fighting alongside you, supporting you, so the meaning is companionship in battle. This is rejected, since that did not happen, and the verse was revealed concerning some weak Muslims who, when harm from the disbelievers touched them, agreed with them and concealed this from the Muslims, and by this they became hypocrites. For this reason Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said that the verse concerns the hypocrites. Allah, exalted is He, refuted them with His saying, glorified is He:

﴿"Is not Allah most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?"﴾ This is apparently an conjunction to an implied clause, i.e., "Will their condition be hidden?" and "Is it not...," or: "Are not those who perceive by the light of Allah, exalted is He, aware of their conditions, and is it not...?" The word "a'lam" (most knowing) is either in its original sense, i.e., "Is He, mighty and majestic, not more knowing than the worlds of what is in the breasts of the worlds, of character and hypocrisy, so that they do what they do of apostasy and concealment from the Muslims and claiming to be of them in order to obtain spoils?" or it means "knowing" (ʿālim).

Qatada said: It was revealed concerning those who emigrated and whom the polytheists returned to Makkah. It was also said: It was revealed concerning some believers whom the polytheists took out to Badr, and they apostatized. They are the ones concerning whom Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿"Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves"﴾ [an-Nisa: 97], etc. What preceded is more in accord with what came before in the verse and what followed from His saying, glorified is He:

﴿And Allah will surely know those who believe﴾ — by sincerity — ﴿and He will surely know the hypocrites﴾, whether their disbelief is accompanied by harm or not. The meaning of "knowing" here is recompense, i.e., He will surely reward them according to what they possess of faith and hypocrisy. It seems that the shift of address between "those who believe" and "the hypocrites" is for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil). The apparent view is that the verse is Madani, on the basis that hypocrisy appeared in Medina, and this supports what preceded regarding its being counted among the exceptions (al-mustathnayat). Perhaps whoever says it is Makki relies on the apparent general statement of the consensus about the surah being Makki, and on the fact that the persecution of the disbelievers against the Muslims took place mostly in Mecca; this prevents that view, or he goes to the view that it is among the reports of the unseen (al-akhbar bil-ghayb), so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 12:

﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed﴾ is an explanation of their compelling the believers to disbelief by enticement, after the explanation of their compelling them to it by harm and threat. Their description as "disbelievers" here, rather than as in what preceded, is because the context of the speech is to explain their crime, whereas in what preceded it was to explain the crime of those whom they led astray. The lam is for communication, meaning they said, addressing them: ﴿Follow our way﴾, that is, take the path that we tread in religion. He expressed this by "following" (ittiba'), which is walking behind another walker, treating the course as if it were the traveller in it; or [the meaning is], follow us in our way. ﴿And let us bear your sins﴾, that is, if that following is a sin for which one is held to account on the Day of Resurrection, as you say, or: let us bear what sins are upon you, if there is resurrection and accountability. They commanded themselves to bear [the sins] while conjoining it to the command to follow, for the sake of emphasis in making the bearing dependent upon the following. The original sense of the speech is therefore: "Follow our way, [and] we will bear your sins," with "we will bear" in the jussive as an answer to the imperative, so the meaning would be: if you follow, we will bear [them]. He turned away from this to what is in the sublime wording, for the stated emphasis. Its source is an indication that bearing, given its certainty, is as if it were an obligatory matter commanded by an obeyed commander. The conditioning upon the condition contained in the command is as in their saying:

"Honour me and I will benefit you" — this does not give that [benefit]. The motive for them towards emphasis is encouragement to follow. The word "bearing" here is metaphorical. In al-Bahr: it is akin to standing by what results from the consequences of sin, bearing being on the back and sins being the borne. Mujahid said: "bearing" here is from hamalah (surety), not from bearing a load, end.

The verse, according to what a group related from Mujahid, was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, who said to those among them who believed: "We will not be resurrected, nor will you; so follow us, and if there is anything upon you, it is upon us."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, who said: Abu Jahl and the chieftains of Quraysh used to intercept people when they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and were about to become Muslims, saying: "He forbids wine, he forbids fornication, and he forbids what the Arabs used to do. So return, and we will bear your burdens." Then this verse was revealed. It was also said: the speaker of this was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who said to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "If there is a sin in persisting in the religion of the fathers, then we will bear it on your behalf."

It was also said: the speaker was al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Attributing what came from one person to a group is common, and the discussion of the reason for that has been mentioned more than once before.

Al-Hasan, 'Isa and Nuh al-Qari read ﴿wa-liyahmil﴾ with a kasrah on the lam of the command, and it was narrated from (Ali, may Allah ennoble his face).

﴿And they are not bearers of anything of their sins﴾: a emphatic negation, continuously, since they are bearers of nothing at all of their sins which they undertook to bear. So the ba' is superfluous for emphasis of the negation, and the continuity indicated by the nominal clause is taken into account after the negation. The first min is for explanation, and it is fronted from a delayed position. The second min is superfluous for emphasizing comprehensiveness. This sentence is either a parenthetical insertion or a circumstantial clause.

Dawud ibn Abi Hind read, as reported by Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, ﴿min khatiatihim﴾ in the singular, and he said its meaning is the genus, and what indicates this is its being described by the plural pronoun. Ibn Khalawayh and Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that this Dawud read ﴿min khatiatihim﴾ as the plural of khati'ah in the sound feminine plural with alif and ta'. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned from him that he read ﴿min khatayhim﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a kasrah on the ya'. The kasrah on the ya' should be understood as a hamzah eased between-between, so it resembled the ya', because the rule for its easing is that. 

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed they are liars﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming the preceding negation. It was said that the lying returns to the making of the bearing dependent upon the following, since it is an informative statement; it does not return to the preceding command, since that is performative and lying does not apply to it. This was objected to: the conditioning does not necessarily require being an informative statement, rather it is a guarantee conditioned, i.e., the making of a guarantee upon the existence of the attribute. Hence al-Zamakhshari said: one who guarantees what he does not know he has the power to fulfil is not called a liar, neither when he guaranteed nor when he failed, because in both states he does not enter under the definition of a liar, who is one who reports about a thing other than as it is. He took this as a question about the wording "liars," and answered it with two aspects. The second, according to what is in al-Kashf, is the aspect; its summary: the lying does not return to their not being bearers, so that it could be said that one who guarantees is not called a liar; rather God, exalted is He, informed that they were incapable of what they guaranteed, and despite that they are liars in the promise of making the guarantee upon the existence of the attribute. The summary: whoever promises a guarantee and, if he guarantees but does not fulfil, is not called a liar; and if he does not guarantee, he is called a liar. The first aspect is that God, exalted is He, likened their state, since He knew that what they guaranteed had no way for them to fulfil it, so their guarantee in His sight, glory be to Him, was not in accordance with what the guaranteed matter is, and they are liars in that their report is not in accordance with what the reported matter is. Some scholars said: the lying returns to the report contained within their promise of bearing, namely that they are capable of accomplishing what they promised, and lying, just as it penetrates speech by its explicit content, penetrates it by what its implied meaning necessitates. In al-Intisaf: in God's saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed they are liars﴾ there is a fine point by which the validity of the command coming in the sense of a report is established, for some people deny it and undertake to interpret all that has come about that as based on the original command, and this did not succeed for them in this verse, because He, glory be to Him, followed their saying ﴿and let us bear your sins﴾ in the form of a command with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed they are liars﴾, and denial applies only to reports, end. From this it is known the aspect of their being liars in their saying that, despite their presenting it in the form of a command, but in whether the verse is evidence for what he mentioned there is doubt, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 13:

﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens, and [other] burdens along with their burdens﴾ This is an explanation of what their statement "follow our way and we will bear your sins" entails for them in the Hereafter, namely harm to themselves, after the explanation that it benefits neither those they address at all. The expression of sins as "burdens" is to signal the extreme heaviness of these sins and that they are crushing. The lam (al-lam) is in response to an omitted oath, meaning: "And by Allah, they will surely bear the entirety of their own burdens" ﴿and [other] burdens﴾ "along with their burdens," and these are the burdens of what they caused through misguidance and by leading others to disbelief and sins, without the burdens of those whom they misguided being reduced in any way.

It was narrated by Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Hasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever calls to a guidance and is followed in it and acts upon it, he will have a reward like the rewards of those who followed him, and that will not diminish their rewards in any way. And whoever calls to misguidance and is followed in it and acts upon it, he will have a burden like the burdens of those who followed him, and that will not diminish their burdens in any way."

Awn said: al-Hasan used to recite it as: "And they will surely bear their burdens, and burdens along with their burdens." The indication here is to the independence of the burdens of their own selves, and that these burdens rose up against them and exhausted their effort, and that the other burdens are like an addition upon them. The Glorious text has chosen what is in the wording over saying "and they will surely bear burdens along with their burdens."

﴿And they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection﴾ a questioning of reproach and rebuke, ﴿about what they used to fabricate﴾ meaning what they invented in the world of falsehoods and fabrications, of which their present claim is part.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 14:

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty﴾ years. This begins an explanation of the trial of the prophets, peace be upon them, by the harm inflicted by their peoples, following the explanation of the trial of the believers by the harm inflicted by the disbelievers. It is an emphasis on the denunciation of those who think they will be left alone merely for professing faith without being tested, and an exhortation to them to be patient. For the prophets, peace be upon them, when they were tested by what befell them from their peoples of various kinds of hardships and bore patience through them, then these believers are more deserving and more fitting to be patient.

Apparently the waw is for coordination (ʿaṭf), and it is the coordination of one narrative upon another. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The oath here is remote," meaning that the sworn-by element has been omitted while its particle and its answer remain, for this involves omitting the genitive noun (majrur) while keeping the preposition (jarr). They (the grammarians) said: "There must be mention of the genitive noun." The fa' is for sequence (taʿqib), so the apparent meaning is that he, peace be upon him, remained among his people immediately after being sent for the stated period. This has indeed been stated explicitly in some reports.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "God, exalted is He, sent Noah, peace be upon him, when he was forty years old, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to God, exalted is He. He lived after the Flood sixty years until the people multiplied and spread."

According to this report, his lifespan, peace be upon him, would be a thousand and fifty years. It has been said that he, peace be upon him, lived longer than that.

Ibn Jarir narrated from ʿAwn ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: "God, exalted is He, sent Noah, peace be upon him, to his people when he was three hundred and fifty years old, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty
Page 143
years, then he lived after that three hundred and fifty years, so his lifespan would be one thousand six hundred and fifty years."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "Noah's lifespan, peace be upon him, before he was sent to his people and after he was sent, was one thousand seven hundred years."

And from Wahb, that he, peace be upon him, lived one thousand four hundred years.

In Jami' al-Usul: his period of prophethood was nine hundred and fifty years, and he lived after the Deluge (al-Gharaq) fifty years. It has been said: two hundred years. The duration of the Flood was six months, ending on the day of ʿAshura.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: It is possible that what God, mighty and majestic, mentioned is the duration of his stay, peace be upon him, from his birth until the drowning of his people. It has been said: it is possible that this is his entire lifespan, peace be upon him. It is not hidden that what is apparent from the sequential fa' is what was mentioned earlier.

It is reported in some reports that he, peace be upon him, was the longest-lived of the prophets, peace be upon them. Ibn Abi al-Dunya in his book Dhamm al-Dunya narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Angel of Death came to Noah, peace be upon both of them, and said: "O longest-lived of the prophets, how did you find the world and its pleasure?" He said:

"Like a man who entered a house that has two doors, stood in the middle of the door for a moment, then went out through the other door."

Perhaps the purpose of the noble wording regarding the statement of the duration of his stay, peace be upon him, is to indicate the completeness of the number and that it is specified explicitly without figurative usage, for nine hundred and fifty may be applied to what is close to it. And there is in mentioning the thousand an evocation of the length of the period, since it is the first thing to strike the hearing. The purpose of the story is to console the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and to strengthen him in what he endured of the afflictions inflicted by the disbelievers, and to show the feebleness of the opinion of those who think they will be left without being tested. The disagreement of those who distinguish (in these matters) is due to the awkwardness of repetition in such speech.

The subtle point in choosing sanah (year) first is that it is used for hardship and drought, unlike ʿam (year), so the choice of sanah fits the time of the call, in which he, peace be upon him, endured what he endured from his people.

﴿So the Flood seized them﴾, that is, immediately after the completion of the stated period. The word ṭufan may be applied to anything that surrounds a thing in abundance and intensity, such as flood, wind or darkness. Al-ʿAjjaj said:

"Until, when its day grew dim, and the flood of darkness covered the dusk."

It has come to predominate for the flood of water, and this is what is meant here. ﴿While they were wrongdoers﴾, that is, while they were persisting in wrongdoing, not affected by what they heard from Noah, peace be upon him, of the signs, and not refraining from their disbelief and sins during this period.

﴿So We rescued him﴾, that is, Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿and the companions of the Ark﴾, that is, those who boarded it with him from among his children and followers. They were eighty in number. It is said they were seventy-eight, half of them males and half of them females, among them the sons of Noah: Sam, Ham and Japheth, and their wives. It is reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq that they were ten: five men and five women.

It is also narrated with a raised (marfu') chain that "they were eight: Noah, his household, and his three sons."

That is, along with their families. ﴿And We made it﴾, that is, the Ark, ﴿a sign for the worlds﴾, a lesson and an admonition for them, because it remained for a long time upon al-Judi (Mount Judi) where passers-by could see it, and because of its fame among the people. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the incident and the story understood from what precedes it, and it is a lesson for the worlds because of its fame among them.

[Page 144]

﴿And Abraham﴾ is in the accusative by the implied verb "remember" (udhkur), coordinated with what precedes it, as a story coordinated with a story. There is no problem in their differing in form, one being a report and the other an imperative. The "idh" in His words, exalted is He, ﴿when he said to his people﴾, is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion, a apposition in which the second term is included within the first) from it, because times contain what occurs in them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted this, but Abu Hayyan objected that "idh" is indeclinable and therefore cannot be an object, while substitution requires that it be one. He then stated that if "idh" is a temporal adverb referring to the past, it cannot validly govern "udhkur", because the future cannot occur in the past, so one may not say "qum amsi" (stand up yesterday). But if it is stripped of its past-time adverbial sense and used flexibly, it may be an object and governed by "udhkur". Others permitted that it be in the accusative by coordination with "Noah", so that it is as if it were said: "And We sent Abraham." Then "idh" is a temporal adverb for the sending, and the meaning, according to what has been said, is: We sent him when his intellect had matured, he was able to reflect and reason, and he rose from the rank of perfection to the degree of perfecting others, when he undertook to guide creation to the path of truth. This, according to what some of the scholars of verification (muhaqqiqun) said, is because the statement mentioned within the scope of "idh" was made by him, peace be upon him, after he reached adolescence and before the sending. But you know that His words, exalted is He, ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you denied, and upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 18], etc., if it is from his words, peace be upon him, to his people, is almost explicit that the statement related from him, peace be upon him, was after the sending. In the Sa'di marginal notes it is stated that this is an indication to rebut what might be said: the call comes after the sending, while what is understood from the verse is that it precedes it. Its substance is that the call intended here is not the result of the sending but the result of perfect intellect and complete reflection. Moreover, the verse's indication that it precedes the sending is not granted, so there is room in the matter. It is also possible that the purpose is to indicate his prompt compliance, peace be upon him. End of quote. So reflect.

Abu al-Baqa' and Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it be in the accusative by coordination with the object of "anjaynahu" (We delivered him), but that is, as you see, weak. What is more fitting, God willing, with His words, exalted is He, ﴿and to Midian, their brother Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf: 85; Hud: 84; al-'Ankabut: 36], is that the accusative is by coordination with "Noah". Abu Hanifa, al-Nakha'i, Abu Ja'far and Ibrahim read it in the nominative, on the basis that the implied sense is: "and among the messengers is Abraham". It was also said that the implied sense is: "and among what is worth mentioning is Abraham", and it was said that it is: "and among those whom We delivered is Abraham". According to the first, the reliance is on the indication of what precedes and what follows it. The implied element is connected to this: ﴿when he said to his people: worship God﴾ alone, ﴿and fear Him﴾ lest you associate with Him, glorified is He, anything. ﴿That﴾ i.e. what has been mentioned of worship and piety, ﴿is better for you﴾ than everything in which there is goodness, or better than what you are upon, on the assumption of goodness in it according to your belief. It is also permissible for "khayr" to be an adjective rather than a comparative. ﴿If you know﴾ i.e. good and evil and distinguish one from the other, or: if you know anything of things in some way, for that is sufficient for judging the goodness of what has been mentioned of worship and piety.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, you worship besides Allah only idols﴾ is an explanation of the falsehood of their religion and its wickedness in itself, after the explanation of its wickedness in relation to the true religion. That is, what you worship besides Him, exalted is He, are only idols which, in themselves, are images made by you, having no attribute other than that. ﴿And you fabricate a lie﴾ means: and you lie, a lie, in that you call them gods and claim that they are your intercessors with Allah, glorified is He; or [it means] you make them and carve them for falsehood and lying. The lam here is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), for they did not make them for the sake of lying. It is also permissible that this be by way of mockery (tahakkum). Some of the eminent scholars said: The more apparent reading is that ifkan (إفكًا) is the direct object, and what is meant by it is the idols themselves, and making them "a lie" is hyperbole; or ifk (الإفك) is in the sense of al-ma'fuk (المأفوك), that which is turned away from what it is, and its application to the idols is because they are made, while they make them into creators. ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and al-Sulami, and ʿAwn al-ʿAqili, and ʿUbada, and Ibn Abi Layla, and Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, read «(takhallaqun)» with a fatha on the ta', the kha' and the lam, with shaddah. Ibn Mujahid said: It was also related from Ibn al-Zubayr, and its origin is tatakhallaqun, from which one of the two ta's was elided; it is from takhallaqa in the sense of takdhib (to lie), and the form of effort (taqallum) is for emphasis. Some claimed it is permissible that tafaʿʿala be in the sense of fa'ala. Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, also read «tukhalliqun» from khallaqa with shaddah, for intensification in creation, in the sense of lying and fabrication. Ibn al-Zubayr and Fudayl ibn Zurqan read «afikan» with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the fa', as a verbal noun like al-kadhib and al-la'ib, or as an adjective like al-hadhar, occurring as an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a creation that is afik, that is, possessing afak (falsehood). ﴿Indeed, those whom you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾ is an explanation of the wickedness of what they worship, in that it hardly benefits them in any way. ﴿Provision (rizq)﴾ may be a verbal noun, object of yamlikun, and the meaning is: they are not able to provide you with any portion of provision; or it may mean "that which is provided," i.e., they are not able to grant any portion of provision. It is permissible, on the reading of it as a verbal noun, that it be an absolute object of yamlikun in its meaning, and also of an implied word, the original being: they do not possess the ability to provide you with provision, and this is as you see. It is indefinite (nukkira). Some of the eminent scholars said: it is for minimization and belittling, as hyperbole in negation; and he specified provision for its high status among creation. ﴿So seek provision from Allah﴾, that is, all of it, on the basis that the definiteness of "provision" is for totality (al-istighraq). Al-Tibi said: This is among the places where the repeated definite noun is not the same as the first; and it is permissible that it be the same as the first, on the basis that each of them is totalizing. ﴿And worship Him﴾, mighty and majestic, alone; ﴿and be grateful to Him﴾ for His bounties, seeking your aims through His worship, bound by thanks to Him, exalted is He, for increase, and drawing by it toward more. The two sentences refer to what precedes them. It is also permissible that they refer to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾, as if it were said: prepare yourselves for meeting Him, exalted is He, through worship and gratitude, for to Him you will be returned. Some of the verifiers said this sentence may be a conclusion (tadhyil) to the sentence before it, of what was related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, or to its beginning; the meaning being: to Him, exalted is He, and not to other than Him, glorified is He, you will be returned, by death and then by resurrection; so do what I have commanded you. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion to establish the wickedness, as you have heard. It has also been read «tarji'un» with a fatha on the ta', from raja'a, ruju'an.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 18:

﴿And if you deny⁠﴾ is conjoined to an implied clause, the sense of which is: "So if you believe me, you have indeed attained the happiness of both abodes. And if you deny," that is, deny me regarding what I have informed you of, namely that you will be returned to Him, the Exalted, through resurrection. ﴿Then surely nations before you have denied⁠﴾ — and this is in reality a justification for the answer, and the underlying sense is: "So do not harm me by your denial, for nations before you denied their messengers, namely Shith, Idris, Nuh, Hud and Salih, peace be upon them, and their denial did not harm them in the least; it only harmed themselves, in that it brought upon them the punishment that befell them. So likewise is your denial of me." ﴿And the Messenger is only responsible for clear conveyance⁠﴾ — that is, the conveyance which leaves no doubt with it, and he is not obliged to make his people believe him at all. I have been discharged of the duty of conveyance with what admits of no addition, so your denial after that will not harm me at all.

This verse, namely ﴿And if you deny⁠﴾ etc., according to what we have mentioned, is part of the account of Abraham, peace be upon him, and likewise what follows it, according to what has been said, up to His saying, the Exalted: (ما كانَ جَوابَ قَوْمِهِ) [al-A'raf: 82; al-Naml: 56; al-'Ankabut: 24, 29]. It has also been permitted that this be an interjection, mentioning the affair of the Prophet ﷺ and Quraysh, demolishing their doctrine and warning concerning the evil of their conduct, placed between the two ends of the story, inasmuch as its purpose is to console the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to relieve him by showing that his father, the Friend of the Merciful, was tried with something similar to what he was tried with from the polytheism and denial of his people, and by comparing his situation among them with the situation of Abraham, peace be upon them both. They said:

In ﴿And if you deny⁠﴾ there is an interjection, and the address in it is from Him, the Exalted, or from the Prophet ﷺ, in the sense of: "And say to Quraysh: 'If you deny⁠'" etc.

Some of the researchers went to the view that His saying, the Exalted: (إنْ تُكَذِّبُوا) etc. is from the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, and His saying, glorified be He:

[Page 146]

﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation?﴾ and so on. This is a resumed statement, directed from Him, the Exalted, as a rebuke for their denial of resurrection despite the clarity of its proof. The interrogative particle (hamzah) expresses disapproval of their not having seen, which requires affirmation. The conjunction waw is for coordination with an implied clause, meaning: "Did they not look and not know the manner in which Allah, the Exalted, originates creation, from material and from non-material?" That is, they have indeed known this.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, according to one of the two transmitted readings from him, recited "ألَمْ تَرَوْا" (Have you not seen?) with the second-person address (ta' of address). According to what this group said, this is for the intensification and emphasis of the rebuke, and it does not require postulating an implied "saying" (qawl). As for one who does not take this as a resumed statement directed from Him, the Exalted, as a rebuke for their denial of resurrection, he said: the address is on the basis of an implied "saying," meaning: "Their messengers said to them: 'Have you not seen?'"

This was justified on the grounds that the pronoun in ﴿Have they not seen?﴾, according to the third-person reading, refers to the nations in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿nations before you﴾. Therefore it is also made to refer to it in the second-person reading, so that the meanings of the two readings coincide. In that case, it requires postulating a "saying," so as to relate the address of their messengers to them, since there is no room for the address without it.

It has also been said: that is because it is not permissible for the address to be to those who deny the return from the community of Abraham or from our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon them both, and they are the ones addressed by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and if you deny﴾, because the interrogative is for rebuke, meaning: "They have indeed seen," so it does not suit

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth﴾ etc., because the addressees in it are the first addressees. That is: if the seeing is cognitive ('ilmiyya), then the command to travel and observe is not fitting for one who has already gained knowledge of how creation occurs. The claim that the first is an evidence from within the self (anfusi) and the second from the horizons (afaqi) contradicts the apparent meaning in several respects. End. So reflect. Perhaps the more apparent and the further from idle talk (qil wa-qal) in the arrangement of the verses is what we have transmitted from some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin).

Al-Zubayri, Isa and Abu 'Amr, according to one of two reports from him, read ﴿kayfa yabda'u﴾ as the imperfect of the triliteral verb bada'a, with the hamza replaced by an alif, as mentioned by al-Hamdani. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He will bring it back﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Have they not seen﴾, not to ﴿yubdi'u﴾ (He originates). This is because, if the seeing is visual (basariyya), it falls on the origination and not on the return, so if it were conjoined to ﴿yubdi'u﴾ it would not be correct. Likewise if the seeing is cognitive, because the purpose is to infer the return from what they know of the states of origination, in order to establish it. So if it were already known to them, it would be obtaining what is already obtained (tahsil al-hasil).

It has been permitted to conjoin it to ﴿yubdi'u﴾, by interpreting the return (i'adah) as His bringing into being, every year, the like of what He brought into being in the previous year, of plants, fruits and other things. For that is among the things by which the soundness of the resurrection and its occurrence are inferred, as is said, without doubt. And it is reported from Muqatil that "creation" here means the night and the day, but this is not correct. ﴿Indeed that﴾, that is, what has been mentioned of the return, ﴿for Allah is easy﴾. It has been permitted that the referent is what has been mentioned of the two matters, ﴿for Allah is easy﴾, since the act of the Exalted does not need anything outside His essence, Mighty and Majestic is He.

﴿Say: Travel through the earth﴾ is a command to Abraham, peace be upon him, that he say this to his people, according to some of the verifiers. Likewise, so did those who made all that precedes of the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, the context. And whoever made His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you deny﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So there was not the answer of his people﴾ a parenthetical (i'tiradan) statement, made this a command to our Prophet ﷺ to say this to the Quraysh.

It has been permitted to make the arrangement of the preceding verses follow what is reported from some of the verifiers, and to make this a command to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to say this to them. For they are like the people of Abraham, peace be upon him, and the nations before them in denying the resurrection and rejecting it. And what is within the scope of this saying contains what indicates its soundness. The non-unity of this with what precedes does no harm. In any case, the attribution of mercy (rahmah) to the first person pronoun in what comes later, if Allah wills, is because that is the quotation of His speech, Mighty and Majestic is He, in its own form, and the like of it in the noble Qur'an is abundant.

Travel (al-sayr), as al-Raghib said, is passing through the earth. On this reading there is tajrid (abstraction, a rhetorical device) in the verse. The apparent meaning is that it refers to passing through with the body. It has been permitted that it refers to circulating thought (ijalat al-fikr). Some have understood this in the sense of what is reported in the description of the prophets, peace be upon them, that their bodies are moving on the earth while their hearts roam in the malakut (the realm of divine dominion). Some of them understood it in the sense of diligence in worship that leads to reward. The meaning according to what we said first is: proceed upon the earth and wander through it. ﴿Then observe how Allah began﴾ ﴿the creation﴾, that is, how He created them originally, in different stages (atwar), with diverse natures and varied characters. For the ordering of observation upon travel through the earth indicates tracing the states of the various kinds of creatures inhabiting its regions. On this reading, the mode (kayfiyyah) in the preceding verse differs from the mode in this verse, because the first, as you know, is with respect to the matter and its absence, and this is with respect to the variation of states.

Perhaps the expression in the first verse is in the imperfect, namely ﴿yubdi'u﴾, rather than the past as here, in order to bring the earlier form to presence, because the origination of creation from a matter and from other than matter is more remarkable (aghrab) than the origination of creation in different stages. This is in the sense that the creation of things is more remarkable than making their stages differ. If you consider that the creation of things in the Hereafter returns to bringing them into being out of pure non-existence without a preceding matter, to avoid an infinite regress (tasalsul), and that making their stages differ occurs only after a matter has preceded, even if only in essential priority, which is that in which the difference subsists, namely the essences of things, you will not doubt that the first is more remarkable than the second. For this reason you find that praise of the origination itself in the great Qur'an is more frequent than praise of the making mentioned. The form of the verb in the causative pattern (bab al-if'al) has agreed with the sense of remarkableness, for it is not commonly used. For this reason they said that it impairs eloquence, were it not that it occurs together with (yu'idu). Among what brings this secret close is what has been said regarding the reason for the omission of the ya' in ﴿yasri﴾ in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 4], that this is because the night is traversed in it (yusra fihi), it does not traverse (la yasri), so that the deviation from the apparent in the wording indicates deviation in meaning. This is a subtle meaning.

It has been said regarding the reason for expressing it in the manner mentioned that it conveys continuous renewed persistence (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi), and this is built on the second meaning of the verse. Some of them said, regarding the difference between the two proofs: this one is ocular ('ayni) and that one is cognitive ('ilmi), or this one is from the horizons (afaqi) and the first is from within the self (anfusi).

Al-Zuhri read ﴿kayfa bada'a al-khalq﴾ with the hamza lightened by replacing it with an alif, then deleting it in connected speech. Abu Hayyan said: this is a lightening that is not analogous (ghayr qiyasi), as in the line of poetry: "Graze, O people of Fazara, there is no pasture here." The analogous lightening of this is intermediate pronunciation (bayn bayn). ﴿Then Allah brings forth the final creation﴾, that is, after the first creation which you have witnessed. The creation (nash'ah) is origination and making. The expression for the return, which is the point of dispute, as "the final creation", which implies that the beginning is a first creation, is for the purpose of alerting that they are one matter of the matters of Allah, Exalted is He, both in reality and in name, insofar as each of them is an invention and a bringing out from non-existence into existence, and there is no difference between them except in priority and in being the last. So it has been said.

The apparent reading is that it is built on the view that the body is wholly annihilated and then re-created as a new creation, not that its parts are dispersed and then reassembled after their dispersal. Each of these views has been held by some, the evidences conflict, and the question, as Ibn al-Humam said, is speculative (zanniyyah) according to the verifiers.
