In the book al-Iqtisad fi al-I'tiqad of Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali: "If it is said: Do you say that substances (jawahir) and accidents (a'rad) are annihilated and then both are restored, or that accidents are annihilated but not substances, and only accidents are restored? We say: All of that is possible, but there is no decisive evidence in the Law determining one of these possibilities." End of quotation. Ibn al-Humam held that the truth is that both modes occur: the restoration of what has ceased to exist in its very self, and the assembling of the parts that were dispersed.

It may be said that the origination of man and the like is not pure invention and bringing out from the nothingness of non-existence into existence in reality, since he is created from dust and the other elements. The apparent meaning is that his passing away is not an expression for becoming pure non-existence, but rather an expression for his dissolution into what he was composed of, and the return of each element to its own element. Yes, there is no doubt regarding the passing away of some accidents and their complete annihilation. Some parts may be excepted from this, so that they do not dissolve into that from which the composition came, but remain as they were. This is the "coccyx" (ajb al-dhanab), according to the apparent sense of the hadith in the two Sahihs: "There is no part of the son of Adam that does not decay except one bone, and it is the coccyx (ajb al-dhanab), from which the creation will be reassembled on the Day of Resurrection." Its interpretation by what Mulla Sadra interpreted it in his Asfar is of the kind that should not be turned to. In that case, the return is by the composition of what dissolved of the elements and its joining to this part. So it is not pure invention and bringing out from the nothingness of non-existence into existence in reality. Nevertheless, each of the origination and the return bears a complete resemblance to the invention and bringing out mentioned, and by this it is correct to say it of every invention and bringing out from non-existence into existence. So do not be heedless.

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Travel through the earth﴾ and is included with it within the scope of the saying. The difference between them in being a report and being an imperative does no harm, for that is permitted after a saying and what has a place in grammatical construction. It is not correct to conjoin it to ﴿bada'a al-khalq﴾ (began the creation), because it is not suitable to be an object of observation. As for when it means seeing, this is obvious. As for when it means reflection, this is because reflection is on the proof, not on the conclusion. The explicit mention of the Glorious Name and placing it as a subject, with its pronoun in ﴿bada'a﴾, is to bring out greater emphasis in clarifying the certainty of the return, by pointing to the cause of the ruling, for it is the name that gathers the attributes of perfection and the qualities of majesty. The repetition of the predication, and returning what preceded to the requirement of the apparent, need no justification. That the purpose of it is not to establish the return for one who denies it, is therefore why it was not woven in this pattern; this is not conceded.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read ﴿al-nash'ah﴾ with the madd (lengthening), and both are dialects, like al-ra'fah and al-ra'afah, though the qasr (short form) is more common. Its place is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing ﴿yunshi'u﴾, with the extra letters removed, the original being al-in-sha'ah, or by omitting the verb, meaning ﴿yunshi'u fayansha'una al-nash'ah al-akhirah﴾ (He originates, then they are originated the final creation), like His saying: ﴿And caused you to grow from the earth a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ is a justification of what precedes by way of verification (tahqiq), for whoever knows His power, Mighty and Majestic is He, over all possibilities, of which the return is one, cannot conceive of doubting His power over it, nor over its occurrence after He has reported it.

Then know that most of those who deny the resurrection do not claim it is impossible, like the conjunction of contradictories. Rather, their furthest position is to consider it remote. The refutation of these people by these verses and the like is clear, for in them is what removes the remoteness, through origination, which is in what is witnessed more difficult than the return. Among them are those who say it is impossible by reason, so it is not fit to be an object of power. These are the ones who claim that the re-creation of the non-existent is impossible. The refutation of them, after granting that what we are dealing with is the re-creation of the non-existent and not the gathering of the dispersed, is by refuting the proofs they adduced for impossibility. The books of kalam (scholastic theology) have fully treated this. As for the refutation of them by these verses and the like, it is because they contain an allusion to exposing the weakness of the proofs of impossibility. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 21:

﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) explaining what follows the later creation (al-nash'ah al-akhirah), i.e., He punishes after the later creation whom He wills to punish, and they are the deniers of it. ﴿And He has mercy on whom He wills﴾, His mercy, and they are the affirmers of it. ﴿And to Him﴾, glorified is He, and not to other than Him, ﴿you will be turned back﴾, i.e., you will be returned. The sentence is a confirmation of the resurrection (al-i'adah) and a preparation for what comes after it. The mention of punishment first is because intimidation (al-tarhib) is more suitable to the context than encouragement (al-targhib).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 22:

﴿And you cannot escape﴾ (from) His (Exalted is He) enforcement of His judgment and decree upon you, ﴿on earth or in heaven﴾, meaning: by fleeing across the wide earth, or by descending into a place of such great depth and remoteness that He cannot reach you there, nor by taking refuge in the heaven, which is more spacious than it, or which is more protective for whoever dwells in it against the hands of calamities, ﴿in what you see﴾, even if you were able to ascend to it, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], or (by taking refuge in) the towers and high fortresses on its side, as has been said. This, however, goes against the apparent meaning. Ibn Zayd and al-Farra' said: ﴿in heaven﴾ is the silah (the clause completing) a omitted relative pronoun (mawsul, the relative word), which is the subject of an omitted predicate. The sense is: ﴿nor is whoever is in heaven able to escape Him﴾. The clause is coordinated with the clause preceding it. This is weak, because it involves omitting the relative pronoun while retaining its silah, which the Basrans consider impermissible except in poetry, such as the verse of Hassan:

Who among you satirizes the Messenger of God, praises him, and supports him, they are equal.

This is according to its apparent sense in the verse. Moreover, Ibn Malik stipulated for its permissibility that the omitted relative pronoun be coordinated with another relative pronoun that is mentioned, as in this line. It is also weak because it involves omitting the predicate without any need for it. For this reason, some scholars made the relative pronoun coordinated with ﴿you﴾ and did not make it a subject with an omitted predicate, so that the coordination would be between clause and clause. Some claimed that the relative pronoun is omitted in two places and that it is the object of ﴿unable to escape﴾, saying: the sense is: ﴿nor are you escaping whoever is on earth﴾, that is, of mankind and jinn, ﴿nor whoever is in heaven﴾, that is, of the angels (peace be upon them), so how could you cause God (Mighty and Majestic) to be unable to reach you? However, it is clear that this is extremely remote, and the words of God should not be interpreted in this way.

It has also been said that there is no omission in the verse at all, and that heaven here is the canopy, except that ﴿you﴾ is an address to all rational beings, so the angels are included among them. Heaven is then considered in relation to them, and earth in relation to others of mankind and jinn. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿And you have no protector other than God﴾ who guards you from a calamity, earthly or heavenly, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who repels it from you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 23:

﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ That is, in His proofs, both the cosmic (takwiniyyah) and the revealed (tanziliyyah), which indicate His essence, attributes and acts. Thus there enters into them, at the first level of inclusion, the first creation, which indicates the soundness of resurrection (al-ba'th), and the verses that speak of it. Restricting them to the proofs of His oneness (wahdaniyyah) does not suit the context. ﴿And His meeting﴾ which those verses speak of. ﴿Those﴾ who are described by what has been mentioned of disbelief in the signs of Allah the Exalted and in His meeting, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿have despaired of My mercy﴾. That is, they will despair of it on the Day of Resurrection, and this is a threat. Otherwise, the disbeliever is not described as despairing in this world, because he has no hope. The use of the past tense indicates certainty. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is to display the difference between their state and the state of the believers, because the state of the believer is hope and fear, while the state of the disbeliever is delusion and despair. So he does not conceive in his mind either hope or fear. Indeed, when the most frightening thing comes to his mind, his state becomes despair instead of fear, and when the most hoped-for thing comes to his mind, his state becomes delusion instead of hope. So this is an explicit statement of their disbelief and a definition of their state. It may also be that the speech is metaphorical (isti'arah): they are likened to those who have despaired of mercy, and these are the ones who died in disbelief, because as long as life lasts, despair of mercy is not realized, given the hope of faith. Or [it means] whoever is assumed to be in despair of mercy, by hypothesis, indicating their deep immersion in disbelief and their refusal to turn back. Al-Dhimari and Abu Ja'far read «yaysu» without hamza, rather with a ya' in place of the hamza. ﴿And those, for them is a painful punishment﴾. Regarding the repetition of the demonstrative (ism al-isharah), the repetition of the predication, the indefiniteness of "punishment" (al-'adhab), and describing it as painful, there is an indication of the gravity of their state that is not hidden. However, the Imam (al-Razi) said: He, Exalted is He, attributed mercy to Himself, Mighty and Majestic is He, rather than punishment, to indicate that His mercy, Exalted and High is He, precedes His wrath, Glorified is He. You know that in the verse, according to this, there is also an indication of the evil of their state, since it conveys that they were deprived of that great mercy because of the great sins they committed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 24:

﴿So there was no answer from his people﴾ — read in the accusative, as the predicate of kāna (with its subject being) his saying, ﴿except that they said: "Kill him or burn him!"﴾.

Al-Ḥasan and Sālim al-Afṭas read it in the nominative, the reverse arrangement (ʿalā al-ʿaks). What is involved in this has already been discussed in its like-cases. By "killing" is meant killing with a sword or the like, so that the contrast with burning becomes apparent. There is no need to posit that ʾaw here means "rather" (bal). Those who gave the command were either some of them to others, or their leaders who said to their followers: "Kill him, so that you may be rid of him quickly," or "Burn him with fire, so that either he returns to your religion once the fire has harmed him, or he dies in it if he persists in his saying and his religion." In either case, the attribution of what belonged to some to all is present. Here the alternation between his being killed (peace be upon him) and his being burned comes up. It may be that this was said by two groups: some people pointed to killing and some to burning. In the verse ﴿qālū ḥarriqūhu﴾ ("they said: burn him!"), they confined themselves to one of the two things, which is what they did: they threw him (peace be upon him) into the fire and did not kill him.

Moreover, it is not meant that the only thing that came from them, in response to his arguments (peace be upon him), was this shocking statement, as is evident from the apparent sense of the noble wording. Rather, that was what their answer settled upon in the final attempt after much back-and-forth. Otherwise, they had uttered innumerable superstitions and falsehoods.

﴿So God rescued him from the fire.﴾ The fa' is explanatory (faṣīḥa), meaning: they threw him into the fire, and then God, exalted is He, rescued him from it by making it, by His glory, cool and safe for him, as He explained in other places. The manner of his being thrown into it (peace be upon him) and God's rescuing him from it has already been explained. This occurred at Kūthā in the countryside of Kūfa. As for the claim that he is in the well-known place today in the land of al-Ruhā, where there is an image of the catapult and water containing fish that is neither fished nor eaten out of reverence for him, this has no basis.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., in his rescue from it (peace be upon him), ﴿are signs﴾ — clear and wondrous — namely, God's preservation of him from its heat, its quick extinguishing in a short time, and the causing of a garden to grow in its place.

It is reported from Kaʿb that only the rope with which they had bound him (peace be upon him) was burned by the fire. Were it not for the demonstrative (ism al-ishāra) occurring in the midst of the narrative, it would have been better for it to refer to what the story contains: ﴿for a people who believe﴾ — He singled them out for mention because they are the ones who benefit from examining these matters and reflecting upon them.

Abraham, peace be upon him, said, addressing them after God had delivered him from the fire: ﴿You have only taken idols besides God out of affection between you in the life of this world﴾. That is, so that you might show affection to one another and keep close ties, through your gathering together in their worship, your agreement upon them, and your harmony with them, just as people agree upon a school of thought, and this becomes the cause of their mutual love and friendship. The object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu) here is a final aim that results from the action and is an effect in external reality. Or the meaning is: the affection of some of you for one another is what prompted you to take them, in that you saw some of those whom you love take them, so you took them in agreement with him because of your love for him. This is like when a person sees someone he loves do something, and he does it out of love (*mawaddatan*) for him. On this reading, the object of purpose is a motive that drives the action, and it is not an effect in external reality. The intended meaning is the denial that these idols have any benefit or harm, and that what prompts people to take them is the hope of benefit or the fear of harm. It is as if the thing they made the cause for taking them was not considered a cause at all, namely what they indicated in their saying: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], to point out that this, because it is a merely imagined matter with no reality, should not be a motivating cause or a driving reason for anyone who has even a little intelligence.

Some have said: it is possible that the addressees in this verse are specific people, and the speakers of ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ are other people. It has also been said that idols were first taken on account of affection, because there were righteous people who died, and the people of their time grieved over them, so they fashioned stones in their likenesses out of love for them. They continued to venerate them in a general way, and their veneration kept increasing from generation to generation until they were worshipped. So the verse is an allusion to this, and the meaning is: your forefathers only took idols besides God, and so on. Similar examples are many in the noble Qur'an. The second object of *ittakhadhtum* (you took) is omitted, and its estimated form is *ālihah* (gods).

Makki said: it is possible that *ittakhadh* is transitive to one object only, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will certainly receive wrath﴾ [al-A'raf: 152]. This was refuted on the ground that its second object is also omitted there. It was also permitted that *mawaddah* be the second object, with an omitted noun estimated, namely "possessor of affection" (*dhāt mawaddah*), and its being "possessor of affection" is considered in terms of it being the cause of affection. The apparent sense of the words of *al-Kashshaf* is that the omitted noun is the word "cause" (*sabab*). The estimation may also be dispensed with by interpreting *mawaddah* as *mawdūdah* (object of love), or by treating it as the very thing loved, for emphasis. It was objected that making *mawaddah* the second object is problematic, because it is definite by virtue of being in an annexation to a noun that is itself annexed to a pronoun, whereas the first object is indefinite, and that is not permissible because the two were originally subject and predicate. It was answered that the impermissibility of this in their original structure does not necessarily imply its impermissibility in this structure. And if the necessity is granted, then it is not accepted that the second object here is definite by annexation, because it is by extension (*ʿalā al-ittisāʿ*), so it is of the type of the verbal annexation, which does not confer definiteness but only lightens the pronunciation. This is what has been said, and it is, as you see, [weak].

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read *mawaddatan* with the accusative and tanwin, and *baynakum* with the accusative. The correct reading is that *mawaddatan* is in the accusative on one of the two previously mentioned possibilities, and *baynakum* is in the accusative governed by it, or by an omitted word that functions as its qualifier. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ruways read *mawaddatu baynikum* with *mawaddatu* in the nominative, annexed to *bayn*, and *bayn* in the genitive by annexation. The nominative is justified on the basis that *mawaddatu* is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is a *mawaddah*," according to one of the well-known interpretations, and the clause is a qualifier of *awthānan*. It was also permitted that it be the second object, or that it be the predicate of *inna*, with *mā* being a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyyah*), meaning "indeed your taking," or a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted, which is the first object, meaning "indeed that which you took besides God as idols is an affection between you," and the interpretations we mentioned apply to it.

al-Hasan, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Asma'i, and al-A'sha from Abu Bakr, read *mawaddatu* with the nominative and tanwin, and *baynakum* with the accusative. The grammatical analysis of each is known from what has passed. It is narrated from 'Asim that he read *mawaddatu* with the nominative without tanwin and *baynakum* with a fatha on the *nun*. He treated it as indeclinable (*mabni*), because it is annexed to something that is necessarily indeclinable. Its position is therefore genitive by the annexation of *mawaddah* to it, and for this reason the tanwin has dropped from it.

As for His saying ﴿in the life of this world﴾, on these readings there are several grammatical possibilities, which Abu al-Baqa' mentioned. The first: that it is connected to *ittakhadhtum* on the basis that *mā* is a restrictive particle (*kāffah*), and *mawaddatan* is in the accusative, not on the basis that it is a relative or verbal-noun particle, and *mawaddatu* is in the nominative so that it would not result in separating the relative pronoun from what is within the sphere of the relative clause by the predicate. The second: that it is connected to *mawaddah* itself, if *baynakum* is not made a qualifier of it, on the basis that a verbal noun, when qualified, does not govern at all. Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted this connection even if *bayn* is made a qualifier, because the adverb of place gives latitude that is not given to other things, so the verbal noun may govern it after the qualifier. The third: that it is connected to *baynakum* itself, because its meaning is "your gathering" or "your connection." The fourth: that it is made a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of *baynakum*, because it has become definite by annexation. Abu Hayyan criticised these two possibilities after Abu al-Baqa' had been quoted on them, as we noted, saying that they are two grammatical analyses that cannot be conceived. The fifth: that it is made a second qualifier of *mawaddah* when it is given tanwin, and *baynakum* is made a qualifier of it. Makki and Abu Hayyan also permitted this. The sixth: that it is connected to *mawaddah*, and *baynakum* is made an adverbial phrase also connected to it, and *mawaddah* governs two adverbial phrases because they differ. The seventh: that it is made a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in *baynakum* when *mawaddah* is made a qualifier, and the governing element is the adverbial phrase, because the governing element of the one who has the circumstance is the governing element of the circumstance, and *mawaddah* cannot be the governing element for this. Makki said: because you have described it, and the complement of the verbal noun is attached to it, so you would have separated the relative clause from the relative pronoun by a qualifier.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he read: "Indeed you have only taken idols besides God; indeed the affection between you in the life of this world," with the addition of *innama* after *awthānan*, and with *mawaddatu* in the nominative without tanwin and *bayni* in the genitive by annexation. It was analysed on the basis that *mawaddatu* is the subject and *fi al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* is its predicate. The meaning is: indeed your mutual love over them, or your affection for them, is present (or existing) in the life of this world. ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ the situation changes, where ﴿some of you will disown others﴾, namely the worshippers, ﴿and some will curse others﴾, namely the idols. ﴿And some of you will curse others﴾, that is, each group among you and among the idols will curse the other group, since God will make them speak. It includes the address and the pronoun for rational beings, by way of dominance of the address. It was also permitted that the address be only to the worshippers, and the meaning of "some of them disowning others" is disavowal, that is: then on the Day of Resurrection disavowal and mutual cursing will appear between you, O worshippers of idols.

﴿And your abode is the Fire﴾, that is, it is your dwelling-place to which you return and from which you will never come back.

﴿And you will have no helpers﴾ who will rescue you from it, as my Lord rescued me from the fire into which you cast me. The plural of "helpers" is used because it stands in opposition to a plural, that is, none of you has any helper at all.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 26:**

﴿So Lut believed in him.﴾ That is, he affirmed him (ʿalayhi al-salam) in all of his statements, or [affirmed] his prophethood when he claimed it, not that he affirmed him concerning what he called to of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and had not been so before. For he (ʿalayhi al-salam) was far removed from disbelief. As for what has been said, that he believed in him (ʿalayhi al-salam) when he saw that the fire had not burned him, it is a weak report and likewise weak in understanding (dirayah), because on its apparent meaning it implies that he had not believed before, and this is not fitting for him (ʿalayhi al-salam). Some have interpreted it in a manner like what we have mentioned, or [by taking] faith to mean its high rank, which only individuals attain. Lut, according to what is in Jami' al-Usul, was the son of his brother Haran ibn Tarah. Some have mentioned that he was the son of his sister, with a taʾ (the letter "ta") with two dots above. ﴿And he said﴾: Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam), as held by Qatadah and al-Nakhaʿi. It was said: the pronoun refers to Lut (ʿalayhi al-salam), but this is not correct because of the disjunction (tafkik) that it would entail. The clause is a explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), as if it were asked: "What then came from him (ʿalayhi al-salam)?" So it was answered: he said, ﴿Indeed I am emigrating﴾, that is, from my people, ﴿to my Lord﴾, that is, to the direction to which my Lord commanded me to emigrate. It was also said: to wherever I will not be prevented from worshipping my Lord. And it was said: the meaning is "the emigrant from those among my people who opposed me, seeking nearness to my Lord." ﴿Indeed He﴾, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿He is the Mighty﴾, the Dominant over His affair, so He will protect me from my enemies, ﴿the Wise﴾, who does not do any act except that in it there is wisdom and benefit, so He does not command me except with what is good for me.

It is related that he (ʿalayhi al-salam) emigrated from Kuthaa, in the region of Kufa, together with Lut and Sarah, the daughter of his paternal uncle, to Haran, and then from there to al-Sham, and he settled in a village in the land of Palestine. Lut settled in Sodom, which is the overturned city (al-Mu'tafikah), at a distance of one day and one night from the village of Ibrahim (peace be upon them both). His age at that time, according to what is in al-Kashshaf and al-Bahr, was seventy-five years. And he was the first to emigrate for the sake of God, Exalted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 27:

﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ as a son and a grandson, when he had despaired of an old, barren woman. The clause is coordinated with what precedes it, and there is no need to coordinate it with an implied clause such as "We set right his affair." The Exalted did not mention Isma'il, peace be upon him. It has been said that this is because the context is one of favour and the recounting of kindness, and this applies to Isaac and Jacob as we have indicated, unlike Isma'il. It has also been said that it is not suitable to mention him here, because he was tested by separation from him and by being placed in Makkah with his mother, without a companion. Al-Zamakhshari said: he, peace be upon him, is mentioned implicitly and allusively in the Exalted's words, ﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood and the Book﴾, and he was not named explicitly because of the fame of his affair and the loftiness of his rank. This is in addition to the fact that the one addressed is our Prophet (ﷺ), who is one of his descendants and knows him best. By "the Book" is meant its genus, which encompasses the four Books.

﴿And We gave him his reward﴾ for what he did for Us ﴿in this world﴾. Mujahid said: it is by his being saved from the fire, and from the mighty king, and by the good praise bestowed upon him such that every community takes him as their leader. Ibn Jurayj added to that the son in whom his eye was gladdened. It may also be added to that the continuation of prophethood among his descendants. Al-Suddi said: that is his being shown his place in Paradise. Some of them said: it is the granting of success in performing the deeds of the Hereafter. It has been said: it is the sending of blessings upon him until the end of time. Al-Mawardi said:
Page 153
it is the continuation of his hospitality at his grave, and that is not for any prophet other than him. The condition of some of these statements is not hidden. Some of them mentioned that the meaning is "We gave him his reward in exchange for his migration to Us." According to this view, it is not correct to count his being saved from the fire as part of the reward; rather, the giving of a child, a good offspring, the continuation of prophethood among them, and similar things that were his after the migration are to be counted as the reward. The conjunction of this and what follows it, the Exalted's words, ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, means that he is among those who are complete in righteousness. This is a generalisation after a specification: when He had enumerated the blessings He bestowed upon him, both religious and worldly, the Exalted said: "And We gathered for him, along with what was mentioned, the good of both abodes."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 28:**

﴿And Lot⦆ is coordinated with Abraham or with Noah, and the discourse concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when he said to his people﴾ is like that which is in the preceding narrative.

﴿Indeed, you commit an abomination﴾, the act that is extreme in ugliness. The majority of reciters read «Ā’innakum» as an interrogative of disapproval: ﴿(No one in the worlds has preceded you in it.)﴾ It is a resumptive clause affirming the perfection of its ugliness, for the consensus of all individuals of the worlds on abstaining from it is only because it is something from which sound natures recoil and noble souls shrink. Abu Hayyan permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "ta'tūna" (you commit), as if it were said: "Indeed, you commit the abomination, innovating it, not having been preceded in it."

**Translator's notes on terms:**
- *Ā’innakum* (أئنكم): the reading with an interrogative hamza, meaning "Do you indeed...?"
- *Hal* (حال): circumstantial clause, a grammatical term describing the state of the subject at the time of the action.
- *Abu Hayyan*: Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi, grammarian and exegete.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 29:

﴿Do you indeed approach men﴾, that is, have intercourse with them (tankihuna-hum). ﴿And cut off the way﴾, that is, you cut off the road by burdening strangers and passers-by with that vile deed and forcing them against their will. Or: you cut off the path of procreation by turning away from tilth (al-harth) and approaching what is not tilth. It has also been said: you cut off the road by killing and seizing property. And it has been said:

You cut it off by the ugliness of the talk people spread about you. ﴿And commit﴾, that is, you do ﴿in your gatherings﴾, that is, in your assembly where you meet. It is a generic noun (ism jins), since their gatherings (andiyatuhum) in their assemblies are many, and it is not called a nadi (gathering) unless its people are present in it; when they have dispersed from it, the term nadi is no longer applied to it. ﴿Wickedness (al-munkar)﴾.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab (al-Iman), and others narrated from Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And commit wickedness in your gatherings﴾. He said: 'They would sit on the road, pelt the sons of the way with pebbles, and mock them.'" And from Mujahid, Mansur, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd: it is the approaching of men in their assemblies while each one sees the other. And also from Mujahid: it is playing with pigeons, dyeing the fingers with henna, whistling, pelting with pebbles, and casting off modesty in all their affairs. And from Ibn Abbas: it is their breaking wind (tadarrut) and slapping one another in them. In another narration from him: it is pelting with pebbles, shooting with pellet guns (al-bunduqi), snapping the fingers (al-farq'a), chewing gum and using the siwak among people, untying the waistwrap (hall al-izar), abuse, and obscenity in joking.

It is not reported in the story of Lut, peace be upon him, that he called his people to the worship of Allah the Exalted, as is reported in the story of Ibrahim, and likewise in the story of Shu'ayb which comes later. This is because Lut was from the people of Ibrahim and of his time, and Ibrahim had already called to the worship and monotheism of Allah the Exalted, and his affair was well known among the creatures. So Lut, peace be upon him, mentioned what was specific to him: the prohibition of indecency and other things. As for Ibrahim and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, they came after those who used to worship Allah the Mighty and Majestic and call to Him, the Glorified, had died out. Therefore each of them called his people to worship Him, the Exalted. So it is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit).

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful﴾, that is, concerning what you threaten us with of the descent of punishment, according to al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) and others. This clearly indicates that he, peace be upon him, had threatened them with punishment. It has also been said: that is, in claiming that we deserve punishment for what we are upon, which is understood from the rebuke known from the rhetorical interrogation. It has also been said: that is, in claiming the ugliness of that, by the one who utters it, your speech. This answer came from them the first time of the admonitions of Lut, peace be upon him. And what is in Surah al-A'raf, mentioned in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said: Expel them from your town﴾ [al-A'raf: 82], and what is in Surah al-Naml, mentioned in His saying the Exalted: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: Expel the family of Lut from your town﴾ [al-Naml: 56], came from them after this time. So there is no contradiction between the restriction here and the restriction there. This was said by Abu Hayyan, and Abu al-Su'ud followed him. It was objected that this specification requires a revelation (tawqif). It was answered that the content of the two answers indicates sequence, since ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful﴾ is of the type of denial and mockery, and it is more fitting for the beginnings of the admonitions and rebukes; while (﴿Expel them from your town﴾) and the like is of the type of punishment and retribution, and it is more suitable to come after repeated admonition and rebuke that caused their weariness and greater pain, along with their ability to take revenge. This degree is sufficient to claim sequence. It was also said, to remove the contradiction between the two restrictions: what is here is the answer of his people to him, peace be upon him, when he advised them; and what is there is the answer of some of them to others when they consulted about his affair. It was also said: one of the two answers came from the great ones of his people and their leaders, and the other came from others. The apparent practice of some of the eminent scholars requires choosing that each of the two restrictions be taken in relation to the answer he, peace be upon him, hoped for in their following him. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 30:

﴿He said: "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people."﴾ That is, by sending down the promised punishment, ﴿against the people who spread corruption﴾ by innovating indecency and establishing it as a practice for those who would come after them, persisting in it, and seeking to hasten the punishment by way of mockery. He described them with this only as an emphasis in seeking the descent of the punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 31:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the good tidings﴾ — i.e., the tidings of a son and of a grandson (nafilah). ﴿They said﴾ — i.e., to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, within the course of the speech. ﴿Indeed, We are going to destroy the people of this town﴾ — i.e., the town of Sodom (Sadum), which was the greatest of the towns of the people of Lut, and in which, it is said, immorality first arose; for this reason it was singled out for mention. In the use of "this" (hadhihi) there is an indication that it was near the place of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The annexation of ﴿muhlikū﴾ (destroyers) to ﴿ahl﴾ (people) is verbal (lafziyyah), because the meaning is future; it has also been permitted that it be a semantic annexation (ma'nawiyyah), treating that as if it were in the past, for the purpose of affirmation and emphasis. ﴿Indeed, its people were wrongdoers﴾ — this is a justification (ta'lil) for the destruction, on account of their persistence in wrongdoing and their persistence in various kinds of corruption and types of sins. The emphasis in both places is for the sake of giving attention to the matter of the report. And the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, its people﴾ rather than "indeed, they," although the latter is more apparent and more concise, in order to explicitly specify their unanimity in corruption, as al-Khafaji chose.

Some of the scrutinizers (al-mudaqqiqin) said: Indeed, that is to indicate that the source of the corruption of their nature is the wickedness of their clay (khubth tinatihim). Therefore there is in it a subtle indication that what is meant by the people of the town are those who grew up in it, so it does not include Lut, peace be upon him. It has been objected that it is far, very far, for its existence to be hidden if it were near Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as is the apparent meaning of the words of the Exalted:

He said, "Indeed, Lut is within it." It has been said: it is possible that he, peace be upon him, knew what they indicated about the people of the town not touching him, but he wanted to state his situation explicitly so that his heart would be at ease, owing to the completeness of his compassion for him. It has also been said: he wanted to know whether he would remain in the town when they were destroyed or would leave it before they were destroyed. It seems that the use of ﴿إنَّ فِيها﴾ ("indeed, within it") rather than ﴿إنَّ مِنهم﴾ ("indeed, among them") is an allusion to this. The words of some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) imply that his saying ﴿إنَّ فِيها لُوطًا﴾ is an objection (i'tiraḍ) raised against the messengers, peace be upon them, on the ground that there are in the town people who have not done wrong, based on the premise that the apparent meaning of attributing "the people" to it is generality, and that "the people" is understood as those who dwell in it even if they were not born there. Or it is a counter-objection (mu'aradah) to the cause that necessitates destruction, which is wrongdoing, by means of the impediment, namely that Lut was among them, 
Page 155
while he did not possess their attributes. And the reply of the messengers, related in the words of God, Exalted: ﴿They said, "We are most knowing of who is in it. We will surely save him and his family."﴾ is an acceptance of his statement, peace be upon him, about Lut, while claiming greater knowledge of him with regard to the manner (of his situation), and that they were not unaware of him. It is also a response to it by specifying "the people" as those other than him, and his family as an objection, or by stating the time of their destruction as a time when Lut and his family would not be among them, as a counter-objection. In this there is what indicates the permissibility, in general, of delaying an explanation (bayan) beyond the address (khitab). What prevails in opinion is that they meant by "the people of the town" those who grew up in it, as is customary, so Lut, peace be upon him, is not included among "the people." This is strongly supported by the words of his people: ﴿Expel the family of Lut from your town.﴾ Ibrahim, peace be upon him, understood what they intended, and knew that Lut was not among those to be destroyed, but he feared that the destruction of his people would occur while Lut was among them in the town, which would frighten and alarm him.

Perhaps he, peace be upon him, came to this conclusion because they did not mention expelling him from the town of those to be destroyed, despite their knowledge of his kinship to him and his great compassion for him. So he said, ﴿Indeed, within it is Lut,﴾ in a manner of grief and lamentation, as in the words of God, Exalted: ﴿"My Lord, I have given birth to a female"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 36]. His main purpose was that Lut should not be in it at the time of destruction. So they first informed him of their greater knowledge of him, and then secondly gave him what would gladden him and calm his heart, similar to what is in the words of God, Exalted: ﴿And God knows best what she delivered, and the male is not like the female﴾ [Al 'Imran: 36]. They emphasized the promise of deliverance, either to indicate their greater concern for his affair, or to treat Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as one who denies their deliverance of him, because of what they witnessed from him regarding this matter. The deliverance may be understood as bringing him out from among the people, separating him from them, and protecting him from what befalls them, for this meaning is the most complete and perfect one. This agrees with what has been said regarding the words of God, Exalted: ﴿except his wife; she was of those who remained behind﴾, meaning, among those who remained in the town. This is one of two explanations. The second is what has been related from Qatadah, who explained "those who remained behind" as those who remained in the punishment. So reflect. The speech of God, Exalted, has many aspects. Here "the family" has been explained as the believing followers of Lut, peace be upon him. The clause ﴿she was of those who remained behind﴾ is a new (independent) sentence. The discussion of this has already passed, and likewise regarding the exception, so refer back to it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 33:**

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot﴾, those mentioned, after they had departed from Abraham, peace be upon him. ﴿He was distressed on their account﴾, meaning distress and grief seized him because of the messengers, fearing that his people would harm them, as was their habit with strangers. They had come to him, peace be upon him, in fine human form.

It has been said that the pronoun in (bihim) refers to the people, meaning he was distressed on account of his people, because of the great calamity he knew would befall them. The same applies to the pronoun in the following ﴿bihim﴾, but this is not correct. The particle (an) is redundant (zaa'idah) for emphasis of the statement in which it occurs. It emphasizes the two verbs and their connection, which is conveyed by (lamma), so that they seem to have occurred in a single moment of time. It is as if it were said: "When he perceived their coming, distress overtook him without delay."

﴿And he was straitened in regard to them﴾, meaning he was straitened by their affair and by the management of their matter; his (dhar') was narrowed, that is, his capacity was constrained, as in the expression "his hand was constrained." Its opposite is "his (dhar') was broad with regard to such-and-such," meaning he was able to bear it and capable of it, because the long-armed person reaches what the short-armed person cannot reach.

﴿And they said: "Fear not, nor grieve"﴾. This is coordinated with (sii'a), and it is permissible that it be coordinated with an implied element, meaning: they said, ﴿"Indeed we are messengers of your Lord"﴾ (Hud: 81), and they said, etc. Whichever it is, the speaking occurred after they had observed in him signs of impatience on their account, and had seen that he, peace be upon him, was unable to repel his people, to the point that his condition led him to say: ﴿"If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a strong support"﴾ (Hud: 80). Fear is for what is anticipated, and grief is usually for what has already occurred. Accordingly, the meaning is: "Do not fear their ability to overpower us, nor grieve over their intention toward us and their disregard of you." Their prohibition of fear of their power, if it was before they informed him that they were messengers of God, Exalted, is clear. If it was after the informing, then it is to comfort him and to confirm what they had told him.

[Page 156]

Al-Tabarsi said: The meaning is: "Do not fear for us and for yourself, nor grieve over what we will do to your people." ﴿"Indeed, we will deliver you and your family"﴾, so that what befalls them of punishment will not befall you, ﴿"except your wife; she"﴾ was, in the knowledge of God, Exalted, ﴿"among those who remain behind"﴾.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read (linunjiyannahu) and (munjuka) with the lightened form, from (al-injaa'), "to deliver." Ibn Kathir agreed with them regarding the second. The majority read with the emphatic nun doubled (shadd nun al-tawkid), and a group read it lightened. Whichever is the case, the (ka') in (munjuka) is in the genitive position by virtue of the possessive construction (idafah), and for this reason the nun is deleted according to Sibawayh. ﴿Ahlaka﴾ ("your family") is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and We will deliver your family." Al-Akhfash and Hisham held that the (ka') is in the accusative position, and ﴿ahlaka﴾ is coordinated with it, and the nun was deleted because the pronoun has a strong demand to be attached to what precedes it, for the sake of the possessive construction. Some eminent scholars said: there is no obstacle to such a (ka') having two positions, genitive and accusative, and coordination with it is permissible under both considerations.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read (sii'a) with ishmam of the sin toward a (damm), i.e. a rounded pronunciation. ʿIsa and Talha read (suu'a) with a full (damma). This is the dialect of the tribes of Hudhayl and Bani Dubayr, who say in words like (qiila) and (bii'a) "qula" and "buwa'a." To this belongs the saying of the poet:

*"She was woven on two looms when she is woven; she thrashes among the thorns and is not pricked."*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, We will send down upon the people of this town a punishment (rijz) from the sky.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to explain what was hinted at by the promise of deliverance: the descent of punishment upon them. Ar-rijz (lit. "that which disturbs") is the punishment that unsettles the one who is punished, i.e., disturbs him, from their saying: irtajaza, meaning irtajasa and idtarraba (it shook and was agitated). Ibn 'Amir read "(munazzilun)" with the doubled zay (intensive form). Ibn Muhaysin read "rujzan" with a ḍammah on the rā'. ﴿Because they used to commit wickedness (yafsuqun).﴾ That is, because of their well-known, persistent depravity (fisq). Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read the sīn with a kasrah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 35:

﴿And We have certainly left of it﴾, meaning of the town, according to what most commentators hold, ﴿a clear sign﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the traces of its ruined dwellings. Mujahid said: it is the black water on the surface of the earth. Qatadah said: it is the stones that rained down upon them, which the first generations of this community witnessed. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: it is that its foundations are now at its top and its roofs at its bottom, until now, and those with sight deny this. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "We left it as a sign," as one says, "Indeed, in the sky there is a sign," meaning that it is a sign. Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that it is only tenable on the basis of the addition of *min* (مِن) in the obligatory position, as in the verse of the poet:

"I gave him, of her, a robe and a he-goat"

meaning, I gave her a bridal gift (أمْهَرْتُها). Some said: this is like your saying, "I saw from him a lion." It was also said: the sign is its amazing and widely known account. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿منها﴾ refers to the deed that was done to them, and the sign is the stones, or the black water. The apparent meaning is what most scholars hold.

The meaning of ﴿for a people who reason﴾ is clear according to these views, i.e., those who use their intellects for insight and reflection. The verb is treated as intransitive. ﴿For a people﴾ is connected either to *taraknā* (We left) or to *bayyinah* (clear). The second was favored by some. The verses clearly indicate the condemnation and ugliness of sodomy (liwat), which is a major sin by consensus (ijma'), and scholars have stated that it is more severely forbidden than fornication (zina). In Sharh al-Mashariq by al-Akmal, it is stated that it is forbidden by reason, by revealed law, and by nature. The non-obligation of the prescribed punishment (hadd) for it, according to Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is due to the absence of evidence for it in his view, not because it is a light matter. Some scholars said: the non-obligation of the hadd is for emphasis of its gravity, because the hadd is a purification.

As to whether it may occur in Paradise, there is a difference of opinion. In al-Fath it is said: if its prohibition is established by reason and revelation, it will not occur in Paradise; if it is established by revelation alone, it may occur there. The correct view is that it will not occur, because Allah the Exalted considered it remote and abhorrent, saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, you approach immorality that no one in the worlds has preceded you in﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 28), and He called it wicked, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿who used to do the foul things﴾ (al-Anbiya': 74). Paradise is free of such things. Al-Hamawi objected to this, saying: it does not follow that because a thing is wicked in this world, it has no existence in Paradise. Do you not see that wine is the mother of wickedness in this world, and yet it exists in Paradise? There is discussion in this, because the wickedness of wine in this world lies in its removing the intellect, which is the restraint against every ugliness, and this quality does not remain for it in Paradise. This is not the case with sodomy.

In al-Futuhat al-Makkiyyah, in describing the people of Paradise, it is stated that they have no posteriors, because the posterior was created in this world for theExcretion of waste, and Paradise is not a place for filth. Accordingly, its non-existence in Paradise is evident. I do not think that anyone with a true sense of honor would allow himself to be sodomized in Paradise, secretly or openly. The possibility of its occurrence there may lead to a person consenting to it or being compelled to it, since whenever someone desires to sodomize another, the desire must be fulfilled. Although this is not definitive regarding the absolute non-occurrence of sodomy in Paradise, it strengthens the view that it does not occur. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 36:

﴿And to Madyan⁠﴾ is connected to an implied verb, "We sent" (arsalna), which is coordinated with "We sent" in the story of Nuh. That is: "And We sent to Madyan ﴿their brother Shu'ayb, and he said﴾" to them, ﴿"O my people, worship Allah"﴾ alone, ﴿"and hope for the Last Day"⁠﴾. That is, expect it and what will occur in it of various kinds of terrors, and do today the deeds by which you will be safe from its calamity. Or the command to "hope" is a command to do that which hope is consequent upon, the cause being put in the place of the effect (iqamat al-musabbab maqam al-sabab). In the statement there is an implied omitted noun, so the meaning is: "Do what you hope for, by which the reward of the Last Day [is obtained]." It is also permitted that no noun be implied, and that the intended meaning of "reward" is a figurative use of the name of time for what occurs within it. It has also been said: the command to hope for the reward is a command to its cause, by way of demand (iqtida'), without any metaphor in it, through the relation of causality (sababiyya).

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Hope" here means "fear," and the meaning is: "Fear the punishment of the Last Day, from the vengeance of Allah the Exalted upon you if you do not worship Him." ﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief⁠﴾: this is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkada), because 'ath'w means corruption.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 37:**

﴿So they denied him﴾ regarding what his speech contained, namely that if they did not comply with his command and his prohibition, the punishment would befall them. This is the view of Abu Hayyan. It was also said that it concerns his being deserving of being worshipped alone, glory be to Him, and that the Last Day is certain to occur, or something similar. ﴿So the quake seized them﴾ because of their denial of him. ﴿The quake﴾ means the severe earthquake. In Surah Hud it says: ﴿And the Cry seized those who did wrong﴾ [Hud: 94], meaning the Cry of Jibril (peace be upon him), for it is what necessitates the quake, by its agitating the air and what is adjacent to it of the earth. Mujahid interpreted "the quake" here as "the Cry." It was said: that is why; and it was said: it is because hearts quaked from it. ﴿So they became in their home﴾ meaning their city, for "home" (dar) is applied to a city, and for this reason Madinah was called "the Abode of Migration" (Dar al-Hijrah). Or the intended meaning is their dwellings, and the singular was used in place of the plural because there is no ambiguity, since they did not live in one single home. Perhaps there is in this an indication that the quake ruined their dwellings and demolished the walls between them, so they became like one dwelling. ﴿Prostrate﴾ meaning kneeling on their knees, and the intended meaning is dead, according to what was reported from Qatadah.

In al-Raghib's *Mufradat*: it is a metaphor for those who remain (in place), from their saying "jathama al-ta'ir" when a bird sits down and presses itself to the ground; and this also returns to the meaning of dead.

Page 158

﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd﴾ are in the accusative, governed by a verb understood from what precedes, namely His words, exalted is He, ﴿so the quake seized them﴾. The sense is: "And We destroyed ʿĀd and Thamūd." His words, ﴿and it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾, are coordinated with that understood verb. The sense is: "And Our destruction of them has become clear to you in the most complete clarity, from [the standpoint of] their dwellings, or because of them." This is by looking at them when you pass by them on your journey to Syria and back from it. It is also permitted that "min" (from) be partitive. It has been said that both words are in the accusative governed by an understood verb, "remember" (udhkurū), meaning: "And remember ʿĀd and Thamūd." The intended meaning is the mention of their story. Or [they are governed] by an understood imperative, "remember" (udhkur), addressed to him, may God bless him and grant him peace. The clause ﴿it has become clear﴾ is a *ḥiyāliyyah* (a clause presented as a separate, independent statement). It has been said that it is with an understood "say," meaning: "And say: it has become clear." It is also permitted that it be coordinated with a clause that falls within the scope of speech, meaning: "Mention ʿĀd and Thamūd, saying: you have passed by their dwellings, and it has become clear to you," and so on. The subject of "it has become clear" is the destruction indicated by the discourse, or "their dwellings," on the basis that "min" is superfluous in an obligatory position. This is supported by the reading of al-Aʿmash, "masākinuhum" (their dwellings) in the nominative without "min." That "min" be the subject, as a noun meaning "some of," is a matter whose weakness is not hidden.

It has been said that both words are in the accusative by coordination with the pronoun in ﴿so the quake seized them﴾, but the meaning rejects this. Al-Kisāʾī said: they are in the accusative by coordination with "those who" in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And We had already tested those before them﴾. This is, as you see, [weak]. Al-Zamakhsharī did not mention as their governing element anything other than what we mentioned first, and that is what should be relied upon.

Most of the seven canonical readers (al-Sabʿah) read "wa-Thamūdan" with tanwīn, by interpreting it as "the tribe" (al-ḥayy). On the reading without tanwīn, it is interpreted as "the community" (al-qabīlah). Ibn Waththāb read "wa-ʿādin wa-Thamūdin" with the genitive in both and with tanwīn, coordinated with Madyan, as in al-Baḥr, meaning: "And We sent [messengers] to ʿĀd and Thamūd." ﴿And Satan made their deeds seem good to them﴾ by his whispering and misleading, ﴿their deeds﴾ that were ugly, of disbelief and sins. ﴿So he barred them from the way﴾, that is, the known path, which is the straight one that leads to the truth. Reading it as general, to restrict it to what leads to salvation, is far-fetched. ﴿And they were﴾, that is, ʿĀd and Thamūd, not the people of Mecca as is wrongly supposed, ﴿discerning﴾, that is, intelligent, able to distinguish between truth and falsehood by reasoning and reflection, but they were heedless and did not contemplate. It has been said: they were intelligent and knew the truth, but they disbelieved out of obstinacy and denial. It has also been said: they were [those] making it clear to themselves that the punishment would overtake them, through the reports of the messengers, peace be upon them, to them, but they persisted stubbornly until they met what they met.

On the authority of Qatādah and al-Kalbī, as in Majmaʿ al-Bayān (Assembly of Clarification), the meaning is: they were discerning in their own estimation regarding what they were upon of error, supposing that they were guided. Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from Qatādah that he said: that is, pleased with their misguidance. This is an explanation that comes to the same as what has been mentioned. It is also related, as in al-Baḥr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), with "qad" understood or without it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 39:

﴿And Qarun and Pharaoh and Haman﴾ are conjoined to ʿĀd. Qarun is mentioned first because the purpose is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what he encountered from his people due to their envy of him. Qarun was from the people of Musa (peace be upon him), and he encountered from him what he encountered. Or, it is because his condition is more fitting to the condition of ʿĀd and Thamud, for he was among the most perceptive of people and the most knowledgeable of them regarding the Torah, yet his insight did not benefit him at all, just as their being insightful did not benefit them at all. Or, it is because his destruction occurred before the destruction of Pharaoh and Haman, so placing him first accords with the actual sequence. Or, it is because he was nobler than Pharaoh and Haman, owing to his outward faith, his knowledge of the Torah, and his being a relative of Musa (peace be upon him). Placing him first for this reason, in a context of wrath, indicates that such nobility is of no benefit and does not rescue one from the wrath of Allah the Exalted for disbelief. ﴿And Musa came to them with clear proofs, but they acted arrogantly﴾ toward faith and obedience ﴿in the land﴾. This indicates the scarcity of their intellects, for one who is in the land should not be arrogant.

﴿And they were not ones who could escape﴾, i.e., they could not elude the command of Allah the Exalted. It is from their saying: "sabaqa talibuhu" (he escaped his pursuer), meaning he eluded him and was not caught. ﴿Indeed, His command overtook them﴾, i.e., overtook them, so they were caught up in ruin and destruction. Abu Hayyan said: the meaning is "and they were not ones who outstripped the nations in disbelief," i.e., that is the custom of nations with their messengers (peace be upon them). This is not the correct reading. In any case, the apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "kanu" refers to Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman. It has also been said that the clause is conjoined to the implied "We destroyed" mentioned earlier, and the pronoun in "kanu" refers to all those destroyed. In this is a subtle indication of the majestic composition.

﴿So each of them We seized for his sin.﴾ This and what follows serve as a concluding summary (fadhlakah) of the verses that mention the punishment of those who disbelieved and did not obey the command of the one sent to them. Abu al-Su'ud said: "This is an explanation of what the non-mention of their having been preceded by a general statement (ijmal) indicates. What follows is a detailed explanation (tafsil) of the seizing. There is something amiss in the arrangement." It seems he regarded the pronoun in "they were" as referring to those destroyed, whose condition is already known. The placing of the object first is for emphasis on the comprehensiveness and totality. Al-Fadil said: "What is mentioned serves to restrict (hasr), meaning that each one of those mentioned We punished for his own crime, not some to the exclusion of others." He objected to this, saying that "kull" (each) carries this meaning whether it is placed first or last. It is answered that we do not concede that it is understood from it "not some" when it is placed last; it is understood from it only through its being placed first. So reflect. The discussion about the referent of the pronoun in "bi-dhanbihi" (for his sin), in question and answer, is not hidden from anyone who has comprehensive knowledge of what has been said regarding the saying "every man and his plot of land." And their saying: "Ordering (al-tartib) is placing everything in its rank," which is well known among students.

﴿Among them is one upon whom We sent a hasib⁠﴾, meaning a violent wind carrying pebbles. It has been said: it was an angel who pelted them with pebbles, and they were the people of Lot.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It may be that 'Ad is included in this, because the wind by which they were destroyed was severe, and it is not free of pebbles with harmful effects. The hasib is the wind or cloud that is set in motion when it is pelted with something."

﴿And among them is one seized by the Cry⁠﴾. They are Madyan and Thamud. He did not say "We seized him with the Cry" in order to conform with what precedes and follows it in attributing the action to Him, Exalted is He, which accords better with His saying "So each of them We seized for his sin," averting the suspicion that He Himself was the one crying out.

﴿And among them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow⁠﴾, and he is Qarun.

﴿And among them is one whom We drowned⁠﴾, and he is Pharaoh and those with him. Some have mentioned the people of Noah, peace be upon him, as well. It was objected that they are not among those mentioned. It was countered that they are the first of those mentioned in this surah from the earlier nations. Perhaps the objector meant by "those mentioned" those mentioned in sequence, i.e., without an intervening nation whose story did not convey its destruction. The people of Noah, though mentioned first, were separated from their counterparts among the destroyed by the story of the people of Abraham, peace be upon him, which did not convey that they were destroyed.

Al-Nisaburi mentioned that He, by His saying "So each of them..." and so on, established another general statement (ijmal) about the sinners, indicating that they were punished through the four elements. He made what composes them a cause of their non-existence, and what sustains them a cause of their annihilation. Thus the hasib, which is hot stones that fall upon each one of them and pass through to the other side, is an indication of punishment through the element of fire. The Cry, which is an intense agitation in the air, is an indication of punishment through the element of air. The swallowing by the earth is an indication of punishment through the element of earth. The drowning is an indication of punishment through the element of water. End of quotation. What is in it is not hidden.

﴿And Allah was not one to wrong them⁠﴾, meaning that Allah, Exalted is He, did not intend to wrong them, and that would be by punishing them without a crime, since that contradicts what wisdom requires.

In Anwar al-Tanzil (al-Baydawi): meaning that He, Exalted is He, would not deal with them as a wrongdoer would, punishing them without a crime, since that is not part of His custom, Mighty and Majestic is He. This indicates that if He were to punish them without a crime, it would not be wrong, since He, Exalted is He, is the Owner of the dominion and disposes of it as He wills. So He may reward the disobedient and punish the obedient. This is a well-known position among the Ash'arites, and the discussion in verifying it is to be sought in the science of theology (ilm al-kalam). We have already set forth, in explaining His saying, "He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned" (al-Anbiya' 23), what will benefit you in this context to recall, so recall it.

﴿But they were wronging themselves⁠﴾, by persisting in engaging in what necessitates that, namely disbelief and disobedience, by their own choice.

Our master, Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, said in substance: The wrongdoing of the disbelievers against themselves is only due to the poor predisposition (isti'dad) in which they are in reality, without any role of making (ja'l) in it. And through the tongue of that predisposition they asked the Absolute Benefactor, Majestic and Exalted, for what became a cause of the manifestation of their wretchedness. End of quotation. The discussion on this is long in its ramifications, so it should be sought in its proper place.

And the placing of the object first is for the sake of observing the rhyme-endings of the verses (ri'ayat ru'us al-ay).
