"The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah" (﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أوْلِياءَ﴾) is an *isti'naf* (a resumptive sentence, one that begins a new statement) containing a condemnation of the state of those destroyed wrongdoers who wronged themselves, and of their like among those who took as their ally someone other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It also points to the greatest kind of their wrongdoing. Therefore, the relative pronoun refers to all the polytheists who worshipped idols besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It is also permissible that it refers to everyone who took something other than Him, exalted is He, as a reliance and a support, whether that was a deity or something else. For this reason, He switched to "protectors" (*awliya'*) in place of "deities," meaning their attribute or their likeness: ﴿كَمَثَلِ العَنْكَبُوتِ﴾ "like the spider," meaning like its attribute or its likeness.

﴿اتَّخَذَتْ بَيْتًا وإنَّ أوْهَنَ البُيُوتِ لَبَيْتُ العَنْكَبُوتِ﴾ "takes a house, and indeed the weakest of houses is the spider's house." This is an explanation of the attribute of the spider on which the matter of the comparison depends. According to what is reported from al-Akhfash (an early grammarian), the sentence is required to stop at "the spider," and the sentence is then a new sentence for this purpose. "And indeed the weakest of houses" and so on is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the subject of "takes" (*ittakhadhat*), the pronoun hidden within it. It is also permissible that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to its object, on the basis of the permissibility of a circumstantial clause coming from an indefinite noun. On both views, the explicit noun is placed in the position of the pronoun referring back to the one with the circumstantial clause, and the sentence is part of the description.

The *lam* in "al-buyut" (the houses) is for totality (*istighraq*, all-inclusiveness). The meaning is: the parable of those who take protectors for themselves other than Allah, in their taking them, is like the parable of the spider, because it took for itself a house, while the weakest and most feeble of all houses is its house. These people took for themselves protectors other than Allah, while the weakest and most feeble of all protectors are their protectors. If you wish, you may say: it took a house that is extremely weak, and these took for themselves, or a support, that is extremely weak. So they and it share in taking what is extremely weak within its category.

It is also permissible that the clause "took" (*ittakhadhat*) is a circumstantial clause relating to "the spider," with *qad* implied or not implied, or that it is a descriptive clause for it, because the *al* in it is for the genus. Scholars have permitted both views for clauses that come after a noun defined by the genus *al*, as in the words of God, Exalted: ﴿كَمَثَلِ الحِمارِ يَحْمِلُ أسْفارًا﴾ "like the donkey that carries books" (62:5). From al-Farra' (a grammarian of Kufa): the clause is a relative clause (*silah*) of a deleted relative pronoun that serves as a description of "the spider," meaning "that which took." He explained the verse we mentioned on this basis. Ibn Duraystawayh (a grammarian) chose the deletion of the relative pronoun in such cases. According to this view, one does not stop at "the spider." You know that making the clause a description is more apparent.

The meaning then is: the parable of the polytheist who worshipped an idol, compared with the monotheist who worshipped Allah, Exalted, is like the parable of a spider that took a house, compared with a man who built a house of baked brick and gypsum, or who hewed it from rock. Just as the weakest of houses, when you examine them house by house, is the spider's house, so too the weakest of religions, when you examine them religion by religion, is the worship of idols. This is a fine view that al-Zamakhshari mentioned concerning the verse, and in it the division of the comparison (*tafriq al-tashbih*) has been taken into account. The purpose is to show the difference between those who take and what is taken, along with depicting the weakening of the matter of one of them and the consolidating of the other's matter in passing. Based on this, the words of God, Exalted, "And indeed the weakest of houses" may be a circumstantial clause, since it is part of the comparison, or it may be a parenthetical clause (*i'tiradiyyah*), since if it were not stated, there would be within it something that guides to this meaning. This is what al-Tibi (a commentator) held, along with the view that it is a circumstantial clause.

The author of al-Kashf (a commentary on al-Kashshaf) said: al-Zamakhshari's statement is closer to it being a parenthetical clause, because his saying "And just as the weakest of houses..." and so on contains no indication restricting the first. Abu Hayyan (a commentator) objected to this view, saying that the wording of the verse does not indicate it, and that it is merely loading the wording with what it cannot bear, as is his habit in many of his interpretations. This is a rash claim against the author of al-Kashshaf, as is not hidden.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: like those who took protectors other than Allah in what they took as a support and reliance in their religion, and took as their guardian other than Allah, Exalted, is like the spider in what it weaves and takes as a house. On this view, the comparison is of the composite type (*murakkab*, a comparison of whole scenes rather than single attributes). So on the side of the thing compared, taking, what is taken, and reliance upon it are taken into account, and similarly on the other side, what matches it. It considers the comparison of the form abstracted from all of that with the form abstracted from this, by analogy. The purpose is to establish the weakness of their religious matter and that it has reached the ultimate point beyond which there is no further point. The axis of the comparison is that their protectors are, in the position of the spider's woven web, in weakness of state and unfitness for reliance. On this view, the words of God, Exalted, "And indeed the weakest of houses" are a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) that establishes the purpose of the comparison.

It is also permissible that the meaning and the purpose of the comparison are what you have heard, except that this makes the concluding statement a metaphor of the representational type (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*), and what came before serves as a preparation for it. It is as if it were said: indeed, the weakest of what is relied upon in religion is the worship of idols. This establishes the purpose of the comparison by following the establishing of the thing compared. In the earlier view, the establishing was by following the establishing of the thing used for comparison. This is close to the abstraction (*tajrid*) and the strengthening (*tarshih*) of the metaphor. A parallel to this is your saying: "Zayd is a sea in generosity, and the sea does not disappoint whoever comes to it," when the second "sea" is used metaphorically for the generous man. Mentioning both sides only prevents it from being a metaphor if it were within the whole sentence. The former view is preferred, because the custom of eloquent speakers is to establish the matter of the thing used for comparison in order to indicate by it the establishing of the thing compared, and because this is only distinguished from riddles after the comparison has been established.

It is also permissible that the words of God, Exalted, "The parable of those who..." and so on, serve as the first premise, and His words, glorified is He, "And indeed the weakest of houses," serve as the second. What serves as the conclusion is omitted and is indicated by what follows it, as in al-Kashf. The whole indicates the intended meaning, which is establishing the weakness of their religious matter and that it has reached the ultimate point beyond which there is no further point, by way of an allusive metonymy (*kinayah ima'iyyah*). So reflect.

The apparent meaning of "the spider" is the type that weaves its house in the air and catches flies with it, not the other type that digs its house in the ground and comes out at night like other creeping creatures. According to what many have mentioned, this type is one of the venomous ones, so killing it is recommended for this reason, not for what Abu Dawud reported in his *Marasil* (a collection of hadith with broken chains) from Yazid ibn Martad, from the saying of (ﷺ): "The spider is a devil that Allah transformed. Whoever finds it, let him kill it."

For, as al-Dumayri mentioned, this is weak.

It has been said: killing it is not recommended.

For al-Khatib reported from Ali, may Allah honour his face, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I and Abu Bakr entered the cave, and the spider gathered and wove at the entrance, so do not kill them.'" Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned this report in *al-Durr al-Manthur*.

Allah, Exalted, knows best its soundness and whether it is fit to be used as evidence. They stated the purity of its house, because it is not established that what it weaves with is from its nourishment that is transformed inside its body, and because the original state of things is purity. Al-Dumayri mentioned that this does not exit from its body but from outside its skin. In this there is a stretch. I have not verified this matter, and I did not specify whether it is from its mouth, its rear, or outside its skin, because I did not care about that matter, not because it is impossible to reach the truth. He mentioned that removing its house from houses is good, because of what al-Tha'labi, Ibn Atiyya, and others attributed from Ali, may Allah honour his face, who said: "Clean your houses of the spider's web, for leaving it in houses brings poverty."

If this is authentically from the Imam Ali, may Allah honour his face, then so be it. Otherwise, removing it is good because of the cleanliness it involves, and there is no doubt that it is recommended.

The *ta'* in "al-'ankabut" is extra, like the *ta'* in "Talut" (Saul). Its pattern is *fa'lalut*, and it applies to the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. From its use as masculine is the saying of the poet:

"Upon their showers, among them are houses, as if the spider itself had built them."

Sa'di Chalabi (a scholar) preferred that the intended meaning here is the singular, and he went so far as to hold that it is feminine. He mentioned that the feminine was chosen here because it suits showing the weakness and frailty of what it takes.

[Page 162]

Mawlana al-Khafaji (a scholar), in an oblique reference to him, said: the apparent meaning is the plural and not the singular, because of the words of God, Exalted, "those who" (*alladhina*). As for the singular of "house," that is because the intended meaning is the genus. For this reason the verb "took" (*ittakhadhat*) is feminine, not because the intended meaning is a feminine noun.

In the *Qamus* (a dictionary): "al-'ankabut" is well known, and it is also called *al-'ankabatah*, *al-'ankabawah*, and *al-'ankaba'*. The masculine is *'ankab*, and the feminine is *'ankabah*. Its plural is *'ankabutat* and *'anakib*, and *al-'ukab*, *al-'akab*, and *al-a'kab* are collective nouns. This was criticised by saying that what he mentioned after the first is counted as collective nouns with no basis, because *a'kab* cannot be used that way. They also mentioned for its plural *'anakib*. There is disagreement about its *nun*: some said it is original, and some said it is extra, like the *ta'*. Its plural in the pattern *'ukab* indicates that.

Al-Sijistani (a grammarian) in his *Gharib Sibawayh* mentioned that Sibawayh mentioned *'anakib* in two places. In one he said its pattern is *fanacil*, and in another *fa'alil*. According to the first, the *nun* is extra, and it is derived from *al-akab*, meaning thickness. [End of the quoted statement]. Perhaps the closer view on this is that it is derived from *al-'akab* with a *fatha*, meaning intensity in movement. So, because of the intensity of its leap to hunt flies, or because of the intensity of its movement when it settles, it was given the name "al-'ankabut."

﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ "If only they knew." That is: if they knew anything at all, they would know that this is their likeness, or that the matter of their religion has reached this extreme of weakness. It has been said: that is, if they knew the weakness of the idols, they would not have taken them as protectors other than Allah, Exalted.

In al-Kashf: the words of God, Exalted, "If only they knew" apply under all the possibilities, that is, those mentioned in al-Kashshaf, which we have mentioned earlier concerning *iygal* (excessive elaboration). He, glorified is He, showed them to be ignorant in taking them, then He added to their ignorance, exalted is He, by showing that they do not know this clear ignorance, which is not hidden from anyone with even a little understanding. The *law* (if) is conditional, and its answer is omitted, as we indicated. Some permitted that it is for wishing (*tamanni*), so it has no answer, but this is not apparent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 42:

﴿Indeed, Allah knows whatever they call upon besides Him of anything.﴾ This is according to an implied speech: that is, "Say to the disbelievers: Indeed Allah, etc." It was also said: there is no need to imply it, since it is permissible that "tad'una" (you call upon) be by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), to signal anger; but there is a discussion on this.

Abu 'Amr and Sallam read "ya'lamu ma" with idgham (assimilation of the two identical consonants). Abu 'Amr and 'Asim, in one of the transmissions, read "yad'una" with the ya' of the third person (absence), taking it as agreeing with what precedes it. "Ma" is interrogative and in the accusative governed by "tad'una," and "ya'lamu" is suspended from it (ta'liq), so the clause is in the place of accusative governed by it. The first "min" is connected to "tad'una" as is apparent, and the second "min" is for explanation (tabyin). It is also permitted that it be partitive (tab'id).

It is permissible that "ma" be negative, the second "min" be extra (ziyadah), and "shay'" be the object of "tad'una," meaning: you do not call upon anything besides Him, the Exalted, as if what they call upon besides Him, Mighty and Majestic, is, because of its extreme worthlessness, not fit to be called a thing.

It is also permissible that "ma" be verbal-masdariyyah, and it with what follows it is in the sense of a masdar, the object of "ya'lamu" according to its meaning of "ya'rifu" (knows/recognizes), governing a single object, and "min" is partitive: that is, "some of anything besides Him" knows your calling and your worship. It was also said: "min" is for explanation, and "shay'" has the meaning of that masdar, and its tanwin is for belittling: that is, He knows your calling besides Him, which is a worthless calling.

It is also permissible that "ma" be relative (mawsulah), the object of "ya'lamu" in the sense of "ya'rifu," and the object of "tad'una" is its omitted returning pronoun, and "min" is either an explanation of the relative or partitive.

It is permissible that it be extra in this case and what follows it, and what is in it is not hidden.

The speech according to the first two aspects regarding "ma" is a rebuke (tajhil) of the disbelievers who take protectors besides Allah the Exalted, because of what these two contain of negating thinghood from what they have taken as a protector, and the interrogation about it, which is in the sense of negation, since it is a denial. In it is an emphasis on the similar, because the state of their deity not being something to be regarded is appropriate; and for this reason He did not use a conjunction. According to the last two aspects regarding it, there is a threat to them, because knowing their calling and worship is an expression for recompensing them for it, and likewise knowing what they call upon is an expression for recompensing them for their calling upon it. He omitted the conjunction here because it is a resumption (istinaf). It is permissible to intend rebuke and threat in all the aspects.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal), and from it is understood the causal explanation according to the two meanings, for from extreme heedlessness is associating with the One who has this attribute what is not counted as anything; and that the inanimate, in relation to the Capable, the Dominant over everything, the one who reaches the farthest extent in knowledge and perfection of action, is like pure non-existence; and that the One who has this attribute is capable of recompensing them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 43:

﴿And these are the parables; We set them forth for mankind, but none understands them except those of knowledge.﴾ That is, this parable and its like among the parables mentioned in the Noble Book.

﴿We set them forth for mankind﴾ as a bringing near of what is far from their understanding. ﴿But none understands them﴾ in the manner of their excellence and of the benefits they entail ﴿except those of knowledge﴾, the firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rasikhun fi al-'ilm), those who reflect upon things as they ought to be reflected upon.

Muhyi al-Sunnah (al-Baghawi) narrated with his chain of transmission from Jabir: ««That the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, ﴿And these are the parables…﴾ the verse, and then said: "The one of knowledge is whoever understands from Allah the Exalted, so he acts in obedience to Him and avoids His displeasure."»»

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 44:

﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ That is, (created them) in truth, observing wisdoms and benefits. It may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the subject of "created", or it may be that (the phrase) is joined to "the truth" from which there is no turning away, entailing religious and worldly benefits, as a circumstantial clause of its object. For they, together with their containing everything upon which their livelihood depends, are evidences indicating the affairs of Him, exalted is He, which relate to His essence and His attributes, as His saying, exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers﴾, indicating to them the affairs of Him, mighty and majestic, mentioned above. The specification of the believers by mention, despite the generality of guidance and instruction in their creation for all, is because they are the ones who benefit from that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 45:

﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾, i.e., persist in reciting it, seeking nearness to God Most High through its recitation, remembering the meanings contained within its folds, reminding people, and urging them to act upon the rulings, noble etiquettes and praiseworthy morals it contains. ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, i.e., persist in observing it. Since the prayer (salah) encompasses the obligatory prayers performed in congregation, and his command, may God bless him and grant him peace, to establish it included a command to the community to do so, it is given a reason by the words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾. It is as if it were said: "Pray with them; indeed the prayer forbids them from immorality and wrongdoing." The meaning of its forbidding them from this is that, because it includes the various forms of worship, such as glorifying God (takbir), extolling Him (tasbih), recitation, standing before God, Mighty and Majestic, bowing and prostrating to Him, the Glorified, which indicate the utmost submission and reverence, it is as if it says to the one who performs it: "Do not commit immorality and wrongdoing, and do not disobey a Lord who is worthy of what you do. How could it befit you to do that and disobey Him, Mighty and Majestic, when you have performed acts of speech and deed that indicate His greatness and His magnificence, the Glorified, such that if you disobeyed and committed immorality or wrongdoing, you would be like one contradicting his own actions?" By what has been mentioned, the well-known problem is resolved, namely that we see many who commit immorality and wrongdoing yet pray and do not desist from it. For its forbidding them from immorality and wrongdoing in this sense does not necessitate their desisting. Do you not see that God Most High also forbids that, as He, the Glorified, said: ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing and oppression﴾ [al-Nahl: 90], and people do not desist; and the prohibition of the prayer is no greater than His prohibition, the Glorified and Most High. So if there is no necessitation there, how could there be here? I see this problem as founded only on the supposition that a prohibition necessitates desisting, and this supposition is false and an idle fancy, which no intellect attests to and no transmission supports.

Abu Hayyan transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi, Ibn Jurayj and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman that the prayer forbids that for as long as the one praying is in it, and it seems they meant that it is like one forbidding the worshipper, saying to him: "Do not do that as long as you are in it," because when he finishes from it, the sayings and deeds that the prohibition indicated through its magnificence and greatness have ceased. It is related from al-Qutb that he said in answer to the problem: The prayer is established for the remembrance of God Most High, as the Mighty Speaker said: ﴿And establish the prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. Whoever remembers God, Mighty and Majestic, is prevented by that from doing what displeases Him, the Most High, whether little or much. And everyone you see praying and committing immorality and wrongdoing is such that, had he not been praying, he would have committed it even more. So the prayer has had an effect in reducing his immorality and wrongdoing. This, as you see, is [weak]. It has also been said: The meaning is that the prayer is a cause of desisting from that, and this is not universal, since the prayer is in the sense of an indefinite noun, and an indefinite in affirmative form need not be general, so the problem is resolved. According to what we have said, the claim of universality is not harmful. Yes, the prohibition we have mentioned varies according to the variation in the performance of the prayer. It is more complete in a prayer performed with the utmost humility and reflection upon what is recited in it, together with performing its obligations, its required elements, its sunnahs and its etiquettes in its best condition. Its prohibition may weaken until it is as if it does not forbid at all, as in the prayer performed in complete heedlessness and neglect of what befits it, which is the rejected prayer, that is wrapped up as a worn garment is wrapped and thrown at the face of its owner, and it says to him: "May God waste you as you have wasted me." It seems the intention of the one who said that the prayer which forbids what has been mentioned is the accepted prayer is this.

Desisting may also be made a sign of acceptance. Some Imamiyya narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever wishes to know whether his prayer has been accepted or not, let him look: if it has prevented him from immorality and wrongdoing, then to the degree that it has prevented him, it has been accepted from him."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from al-Hasan who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Whoever his prayer does not restrain from immorality and wrongdoing, there is no prayer for him.'" And in another wording: "It has only increased him in distance from God Most High." Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it with this wording from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, as a marfu' report.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, that it was said to him: "So-and-so prolongs the prayer." He said: "Indeed the prayer benefits only one who obeys it," then he recited: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾. It may happen to one who prays much that some of his prayer falls upon the fitting manner, and so it is accepted by God Most High out of kindness and generosity, and the effect of that appears in desisting from sins. To this points what Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, who said: "A man came to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: 'So-and-so prays at night, but when he becomes morning he steals.' He said: 'His prayer will restrain him from what you say.'"

More explicit than this in what we have mentioned is what is reported: "A young man of the Ansar used to pray with the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he would not leave any of the indecencies without committing it. It was described to him, and he, upon him be prayer and peace, said: 'His prayer will restrain him.' And he did not delay but repented." Except that Ibn Hajar mentioned that he did not find it in the books of hadith.

Then, interpreting the prayer in the verse as the well-known prayer is the apparent meaning, supported by the reports and the authentic traditions. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning of it here is the Qur'an. Ibn Bahr said: the intended meaning of it is supplication, i.e., establish the call to the command of God Most High, for the call to His command, the Glorified, forbids immorality and wrongdoing. Each of these is a departure from the apparent meaning without a motive. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that he used to recite: "Indeed the prayer enjoins what is good and forbids immorality and wrongdoing." ﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾.

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Abu Qurrah, Mujahid and Atiyyah said: the meaning is that God Most High's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him, the Glorified. In another wording: "The remembrance of God Most High of the servant is greater than the servant's remembrance of God Most High." It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said this, then recited: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152].

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Malik that he said: God Most High's remembrance of the servant in the prayer is greater than the prayer. So "dhikr" is a verbal noun added to the agent, and the object is omitted, and likewise the one preferred over, which is particular as you have heard. It is permissible that it be general, i.e., greater than everything. It has also been said: the meaning is "And the servant's remembrance of God Most High in the prayer is greater than the rest of the pillars of the prayer." It has been said: i.e., "And the servant's remembrance of God Most High in the prayer is greater than his remembrance of Him, the Glorified, outside the prayer." It has been said: i.e., "And the servant's remembrance of God Most High is greater than all his other deeds." And there is related from a group of the early generations what this implies.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mu'adh ibn Jabal who said: "No son of Adam has done a deed more saving for him from the punishment of God Most High than the remembrance of God Most High." They said: "Not even jihad in the way of God Most High?" He said: "Not even striking with his sword until it breaks, because God Most High says in His Book: ﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu al-Darda' who said: "Shall I not inform you of the best of your deeds, the dearest of them to your Sovereign, the highest of them in your ranks, and better for you than that you fight your enemy and they strike your necks and you strike theirs, and better than giving dinars and dirhams? They said: 'What is it, O Abu al-Darda'?' He said: 'The remembrance of God Most High. ﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾.'"

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Salman that he was asked which deed is best. He said: "Do you not recite the Qur'an? ﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾. Nothing is better than the remembrance of God." It is attributed in al-Bahr to Abu al-Darda'. Salman, may God be pleased with them both, the saying we mentioned first from whom you have heard; and perhaps that is one of two narrations from them. And there came from Ibn Abbas also a narration that suggests the intended meaning of the remembrance of God Most High is the servant's remembrance of Him, the Glorified.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim in al-Kuna and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman transmitted from 'Antarah who said: I said to Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "Which deed is best?" He said: "The remembrance of God is greater. No people sit in one of the houses of God Most High studying the Book of God and exchanging it among themselves, except that the angels overshadow them with their wings, and they are guests of God Most High as long as they are in it, until they turn to another discourse. And no man travels a path seeking knowledge in it, except that God Most High makes easy for him a path to Paradise."

It has been said: the intended meaning of the remembrance of God is the prayer, as in His saying: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], i.e., and the prayer is greater than the rest of the acts of obedience, and He expressed it by that to indicate that what it contains of the remembrance of God Most High is the principal element in its being preferred over good deeds and restraining from bad deeds. It has also been said: the meaning is "And the remembrance of God Most High at the time of immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of His prohibition of them and His threat upon them, is greater in deterrence than the prayer." (So "dhikr" on these sayings is a verbal noun added to the object, and the one preferred over is omitted.) It is permissible that the superlative form not be for comparison, whether the verbal noun is added to the agent or to the object, as in "God is greatest" [Allahu akbar]. ﴿And God knows what you do﴾, of good and obedience, so He will repay you with the best of repayment. Abu Hayyan said: ﴿God knows what you do﴾ of good and evil, so He will repay you according to it; in it is promise and threat and urging toward vigilance.

To You be praise, O God, for what You have bestowed upon us by completing the twentieth part of the Tafsir Ruh al-Ma'ani of the Allamah al-Alusi, and You have granted us success in it. We ask You to facilitate for us what remains of it by Your help and Your power, and it is followed, God willing, by the twenty-first part, whose beginning is His saying, Most High: ﴿And do not argue﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 46:

Page 2

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book⁠ (ahl al-kitab)—﴾ from among the Jews and the Christians. It is said: from among the Christians of Najran. ﴿except in a manner that is best⁠﴾, that is, with the best trait, such as responding to harshness with gentleness, anger with restraint, contention with sincere counsel, and rage with patience, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Repel with that which is best﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96; Fussilat: 34]. ﴿except for those of them who have wronged⁠﴾, by transgressing and obstinacy, who did not accept sincere counsel and for whom gentleness did not avail, so harshness was used with them.

Ibn Jarir narrated, on the authority of Mujahid, that those who did wrong were those who ascribed a son and a partner (to Allah), or who said: "The hand of Allah is chained," or: "Allah is poor," or who harmed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This harshness, which the verse indicates is permitted, does not extend to fighting against those wrongdoers among the People of the Book in any of the mentioned forms of their wrongdoing, because the apparent fact that the surah is Meccan implies that this verse is Meccan, and fighting was not, according to the well-known view, legislated in Mecca. Harshness is not confined to fighting, as is clear.

It was also said that the meaning is: Do not argue with those who have entered the dhimmah (protected status) and pay the jizyah (poll tax), except in a manner that is best, except for those who have wronged, who have broken the dhimmah and withheld the jizyah; for them, the argument is with the sword.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something close to this from Mujahid. It has been objected that the surah is Meccan, and war and jizyah were legislated in Medina, and that the verse being an explanation of a ruling yet to come is a far-fetched notion; moreover, there is no indication for the specification.

It was said: it is possible that the one who says this holds that the verse is Medinan while the surah is Meccan by consideration of the majority of its verses; or that he is one who says that war was legislated in Mecca at the very end of the matter, and the surah is the last thing revealed in it, except that it did not take place. The non-occurrence does not indicate the non-legislation.

It is narrated from Ibn Zayd that the intended People of the Book are the believers among the People of the Book; "in a manner that is best" means agreeing with them concerning what they relate of the reports of their predecessors; and "those who have wronged" means those among them who remained upon their disbelief. This is, as you see, far-fetched. There is disagreement concerning whether the verse has been abrogated.

Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from Qatadah that he said: In this verse He forbade arguing with the People of the Book; then that was abrogated when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day⁠﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], and there is no argument harsher than the sword. In Majma' al-Bayan it is said: the correct view is that it is not abrogated, because the intended meaning of argument (al-jidal) is debate (al-munazarah), and that, in the best manner, is the obligatory requirement which no other is permitted.

Some of the great scholars said: the argument "in the best manner" is at the beginning of the call, since it precedes fighting, so abrogation does not follow, nor does the complete absence of fighting. As for the claim that the prohibition indicates generality across all times, which would entail abrogation, this is not sound; it is answered that whoever fights like one who withholds the jizyah falls under the exception, so there is no abrogation, rather it is specification by a connected exception. And the claim that this requires the legislation of fighting in Mecca is not correct, because it is left unmentioned, so consider.

Ibn Abbas read "Alla bi-llati" (with ﴿ألا﴾), taking "ألا" as a particle of alerting and opening, the implied meaning being: "Argue with them in the manner that is best." ﴿And say: We believe in what has been revealed to us⁠﴾ of the Qur'an ﴿and what has been revealed to you⁠﴾, that is, and in what has been revealed to you of the Torah and the Gospel. This statement is a kind of argument in the manner that is best. Sufyan ibn Husayn narrated that he said: this is their argument in the manner that is best.

Al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The People of the Book used to read the Book in Hebrew and translate it into Arabic for the people of Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, and say: We believe in what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you,'" the verse.

Affirmation and denial are not contradictories, so both may be absent.

﴿And our God and your God is one⁠﴾, having no partner in divinity. ﴿And we are to Him submitting⁠﴾, that is, obedient exclusively, as the placing of "lahu" (to Him) first indicates; and in it is an allusion to their taking their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 47:

﴿And thus have We sent down to you the Book﴾. This is a turning of the address (tajrid) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "Thus" (dhalika) points to the verbal noun (masdar) of the verb that follows it, and the distance implied in it (ma fihi min ma'na al-bu'd) indicates the elevated rank of the one referred to in excellence. The meaning is: "Like that sending down, wondrous in its nature and in harmony with the sending down of all the (other) Books, We have sent down to you the Qur'an, of which this verse is a part, which speaks of what was mentioned: disputing in the best manner." It has also been said that the reference is to what preceded, the mention of the Book and its people; i.e., "And just as We sent down Books to those before you, so We have sent down to you the Book."

﴿Then those to whom We have given the Book﴾ from the two groups, the Jews and the Christians, on the basis that the intended "Book" is its genus, encompassing the Torah and the Gospel, and the statement is on its apparent sense. It has also been said that it is elliptical with an omitted genitive (mudaf), i.e., "We have given them the knowledge (ilm) of the Book." ﴿believe in it﴾, i.e., in the Book that was sent down to you. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this, as you see, is far-fetched. The intended ones in the statement of those who preceded are those of them from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) wherever they were, affirming the revelation of the Qur'an according to what they knew from what they had of the Book. The present tense is to evoke that scene in the narration. Their specification with the giving of the Book indicates that those after them among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) have had the Book removed from them by abrogation (naskh). In another view, his contemporaries (peace be upon him) who acted by their Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like, and their specification with the giving of the Book is because they are the ones who benefit from it, so it is as if those other than them were not given it. It has been said: this supports the view that the mentioned verses are Medinan, since if they were Meccan, Abdullah would be among those who embraced Islam after the Hijrah, based on it being a communication from Allah the Exalted about their future acceptance of Islam; and the distinction by consideration of the communication is very remote. Al-Tabarsi permitted that the relative clause refers to the Muslims of this Ummah, and the pronoun (bihi) refers to the Qur'an, but what is in it is not hidden. Perhaps the more apparent view is that the intended are the scholars of the two peoples of the Book, who are deserving that the giving of the Book be attributed to them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. There is no remoteness in the verses being Meccan based on what you have heard. The fa' (then) is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes, for their belief in it is ordered upon the sending down in the mentioned manner. ﴿And of these﴾, i.e., and of the Arabs, or of the people of Makkah, on the basis that the relative clause refers to Abdullah and his like; or of those in his (ﷺ) time from among the Jews and Christians, on the basis that the intended is those who preceded. ﴿who believe in it﴾, i.e., in the Book that was sent down to you. "Min" (of), according to what some have inferred, is partitive and stands in the place of the subject (mubtada'), and it has parallels in the Noble Book. ﴿And none deny Our signs﴾, i.e., and none deny it. This apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun to draw attention to the manifest indication of the Book regarding what is in it, and that it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The attribution to the "We" of majesty is for added exaltation. In what has been mentioned is the utmost reproach against the one who denies it.

Denial (jahd), as al-Raghib said, is the negation of what is affirmed in the heart and the affirmation of what is negated in the heart. Here it is interpreted as denial with knowledge, as if it were said: "None deny Our signs while knowing them" ﴿except the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who plunge deeply into disbelief and are determined upon it, for that prevents them from acknowledgment and submission. It has been said that it may be interpreted as denial in general, and the disbelievers are meant as those who plunge deeply into disbelief as well, by the indication of the implication of the speech and the expression "Our signs" upon that; i.e., none deny Our signs despite their manifestness and the elevation of their status except those who plunge deeply into disbelief, because that prevents them from giving them attention, turning to them, and reflecting on what would lead them to knowledge of their reality. The intended are those who possess that attribute without any specific individual being aimed at. It has been said: they are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions.

﴿And you did not recite any scripture before it﴾: that is, you were not, before Our sending the Book down to you, able to recite ﴿any scripture﴾, meaning a book. Here ( مِن ) (min) is a redundant particle (ṣila). ﴿Nor could you write it with your right hand﴾: you were not able to write it. Or, it was not your custom to recite it or to write it. The mention of the right hand adds emphasis to the negation, from the Prophet (ﷺ), of writing. It is like the eye in your saying, "I saw with my own eye," to confirm and establish the literal meaning so that no figurative meaning (majāz) remains. ﴿Otherwise the falsifiers would have had doubts﴾: that is, if you had been one who was able to recite and write, or one who habitually did both, then the idolaters of Makkah would have had doubts and said, "Perhaps he picked it up from the books of the ancients." Since you were not like that, there was no basis for their doubt. It seems that the possibility of having learned it was not considered, because it is evident that a lengthy, detailed book like this cannot be received and learned except over a long period of time, through a course of study whose like cannot be hidden. He described the idolaters of Makkah as falsifiers (mubṭilūn) on account of their doubt and their disbelief. He, peace and blessings be upon him, was unlettered (ummī). So it is as if it were said: "Then these falsifiers would now have doubted, and at that time there was a basis for their doubt." It has also been said: he described them with this (falsehood) in consideration of their doubt, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, was unlettered; and in consideration of their doubt, though he, peace and blessings be upon him, was not unlettered. As for their being falsifiers according to the first consideration, it is clear. As for their being so according to the second consideration, it is because the most that follows from his not being unlettered (ﷺ) is the absence of one of the aspects of inimitability (i'jāz), and the remaining aspects suffice for the purpose. Thus the one who doubts is a falsifier, like one who doubts the prophethood of the prophets who were not unlettered, and the soundness of what they brought.

The first view is more apparent. That the intended falsifiers are the idolaters of Makkah is what is related from Mujāhid. Qatādah said: they are the People of the Book, meaning: if you had been reciting or writing before this, the People of the Book would have had doubts, because your description in their scripture is "unlettered." As for describing them as falsifiers, it has been said that this is in consideration of their doubt, and he (ﷺ) was unlettered as is the reality. Otherwise, they are not falsifiers in their doubt, on the assumption that he, peace and blessings be upon him, were not unlettered. In al-Kashf: this is a supposition and an illustration of implication, showing that the matter rests on the inimitable (miracle), and that his, peace and blessings be upon him, being unlettered and not writing is not something that would defeat his claim by its absence. That implication does not differ, and the one who denies it is a falsifier. End of quote. So reflect.

Next, it has been disputed whether, after prophethood, he (ﷺ) used to read and write or not. It has been said: he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not write well. Al-Baghawī chose this in al-Tahdhīb and said it is the most sound (aṣaḥḥ). Some claimed that he, peace and blessings be upon him, came to know writing after he had not known it, and that his not knowing it was due to the miracle of this verse. When the Qur'an was revealed, Islam became widespread, and the matter of doubt became evident, then he learned writing at that time.

Ibn Abī Shaybah and others related:
«He, peace and blessings be upon him, did not die until he had written and read.»

This was reported to al-Sha'bī, and he confirmed it, and said: "I heard people saying it, and there is nothing in the verse that contradicts it."

Ibn Mājah related from Anas, who said:
«The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw written on the gate of Paradise: charity is rewarded tenfold, and a loan eighteenfold."»

The ability to read is a branch of the ability to write, and this is refuted by the possibility that God empowered him, peace and blessings be upon him, to read without writing as a miracle, or that there is an implied element in the text, which is: "So I asked about what was written, and it was said..." etc. Hadiths in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and others support writing, as in the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyah: «(The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, took the document, and he did not write well, so he wrote: "This is what Muḥammad son of ʿAbd Allāh has agreed upon..."») the hadith.

Among those who held this view were Abū Dharr ʿAbd ibn Aḥmad al-Harawī, Abū al-Fatḥ al-Naysābūrī, and Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī from the Maghribis. It was reported from al-Simnānī, who wrote a book on it, and Ibn Muniyyah preceded him to it. When Abū al-Walīd said this, he was attacked, accused of heresy (zandaqa), and cursed from the pulpits. Then a session was convened for him, and he established the proof for his claim, and he wrote about it to the scholars of the regions, and they replied with what agreed with it. Knowing writing after he was unlettered (ﷺ) does not contradict the miracle; rather it is another miracle, since it was without instruction. Some eminent scholars rejected al-Bājī's book, citing the sound hadith: «(We are an unlettered nation; we do not write nor do we calculate).» And he said: everything in the hadith that says "he wrote" means an order to write, as one says, "The sultan wrote to so-and-so with such-and-such." The placement of God's saying, ﴿from before it﴾, before ﴿nor could you write it﴾ is virtually explicit that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not write at all. That the intervening restriction refers to what follows is not consistent. Some eminent scholars thought it refers to what precedes and what follows, and said: it is understood from this that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was able to recite and write after the revelation of the Book, and without this consideration the statement would be devoid of benefit. You know that even if what he mentioned about the reference is granted, the matter of benefit is not complete except if the force of implication (mafhūm) is accepted, and the one who opined this does not hold it as authoritative. It is not hidden that his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: «"We are an unlettered nation; we do not write nor do we calculate"» is not an explicit text on the continuing negation of writing from him, peace and blessings be upon him. Perhaps that is in consideration of his being sent while in such a state, and most of those to whom he was sent among the Arabs, while he was among them, were unlettered, neither writing nor calculating. So the non-persistence of the attribute of unlettered-ness in most of them afterward does no harm. As for what was mentioned about interpreting "he wrote" as an order to write, it is contrary to the apparent meaning. In al-Nawawī's commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, quoting al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, it is stated that his saying in the narration we have cited: «"He did not write well, so he wrote"» is like an explicit text that he, peace and blessings be upon him, wrote himself. Turning away from this to something else is a figurative sense for which there is no necessity. Then he said: The discourse of every party on this question has been long, and each party has reproached the other on this. God knows best.

I have seen in some books, and I do not now recall which book it is, that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not read what he wrote, but when he looked at the writing he knew what was in it, through the letters informing him, peace and blessings be upon him, of their names, so that each letter tells him about itself that it is the letter of such-and-such. This is analogous to the foreleg informing him, peace and blessings be upon him, that it was poisoned.

You know that such a thing is not accepted without a sound report, and I have not found one.

**"Rather, it"**, that is, the Qur'an. This is a turning away from their doubt, meaning that the Qur'an is not something to be doubted, because its matter is clear. **"Rather, it is clear signs"**, evident, established and firmly fixed **"in the hearts of those who have been given knowledge"**, without being gathered from a book that they memorize in such a way that it cannot be altered, unlike other books. The phrase describing this community, "their hearts are their gospels" (ṣudūruhum anājīlahum), also occurs. The most apparent reading is that the pronoun "it" refers to the Qur'an, and this is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd): "Rather, they are clear signs" (bal hiya āyātun bayyinātun). Qatada said that the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he read "Rather, he is a clear sign" (bal huwa āyatun bayyinatun) in the singular. Some scholars took it to refer to him (ﷺ) according to the plural reading, meaning: "Rather, the Prophet and his affairs are signs." It was also said that the pronoun refers to what is understood from the preceding negation, that is, his not reciting and not writing, meaning clear signs in the hearts of the scholars among the People of the Book, because that is the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) in their scripture. All of these, as you see, are far-fetched. In the last view, "those who have been given knowledge" is taken to mean the scholars of the People of the Book, which is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Most scholars hold that they are the scholars of the Companions, or the Prophet (ﷺ) and the scholars among his Companions, and this is related from al-Ḥasan.

Some of the Imamiyya (the Twelver Shiʿi school) narrated from Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are the Imams from the family of Muhammad (ﷺ).

**"And none deny Our signs"**, although they are as has been mentioned, **"except the wrongdoers"**, those who transgress the limit in evil, obstinacy and corruption.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 50:

﴿And they say﴾: that is, the disbelievers of Quraysh, at the instigation of some of the People of the Book.

It is also said that the pronoun refers to the People of the Book: ﴿Why were not signs sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ such as the she-camel of Salih and the staff of Musa. Most of the Kufan reciters read "āyah" (sign) in the singular. ﴿Say: Indeed, the signs are with Allah﴾, He sends them down as He wills, with no interference from anyone in that whatsoever. ﴿And I am only a clear warner﴾: it is not my task except to warn with what I have been given of the signs, not to bring what you have proposed. So the restriction is a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb). ﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾: this is a resumed statement, coming from Him, the Exalted, as a rejection of their proposal and an explanation of its falsehood. The hamza is for denial and negation, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Shall I limit myself? Has not a sign sufficed them, one that suffices in place of all other signs?" ﴿that We have sent down to you the Book﴾, speaking the truth, confirming what is before it of the heavenly scriptures, while you are far removed from studying and practicing them.

﴿It is recited to them﴾: its recitation continues upon them, as they are challenged by it. So it remains with them as an enduring sign that does not cease and does not vanish, unlike every sign which disappears after its occurrence. It is also said: ﴿It is recited to them﴾, that is, to the People of the Book, confirming what is in their hands of your description and the description of your religion. This has validity if the pronoun in "they say" above refers to the People of the Book; but if it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, then what is in it is not hidden.

﴿Indeed in that﴾: that is, in this Book of great standing that endures through the passage of ages. It is also said: that which is a clear proof. ﴿is surely a mercy﴾: that is, a great blessing. ﴿and a reminder﴾: that is, a remembrance. ﴿for a people who believe﴾: that is, whose concern is belief, not obstinacy. The prepositional phrase is attached to "reminder," and the verb is meant in the future sense. It is also permissible that "mercy and reminder" are two elements that share the prepositional phrase, in which case the verb may be in the present sense.

Al-Firyabi, al-Darimi, Abu Dawud in his Marasil, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Yahya ibn Ja'dah, who said: "Some Muslims came with a shoulder-blade on which they had written some of what they had heard from the Jews. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Enough folly or misguidance for a people that they turn away from what their Prophet has brought to them, towards what another has brought to others.' Then this was revealed."

[Page 7]

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 29, verse 51:

﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book﴾, the verse.

Al-Isma'ili, in his *Mu'jam*, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from this Yahya something close to what has been mentioned, reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And they believe﴾ on this reading is taken in its literal sense only. It has been objected that the context (al-siyaq) and the preceding passage (al-sibaq) concern the disbelievers, and that the apparent meaning is that the verse ﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾ is a reply to their saying ﴿Why was it not sent down﴾, and so on. Taking the reason for revelation to be what has been mentioned is a departure from this, so reflect.

[Page 7]

On this view, the verse is evidence for those who forbade reading the Torah and similar books. This prohibition is also reported from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abu Mulaykah, who said: 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir ibn Rukn sent a gift to Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. She thought he was 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, so she refused it and said: "He reads the books, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them?﴾" It was said to her: "It is 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir," and she accepted it. Several reports also contain what implies the prohibition.

'Abd al-Razzaq, in *al-Musannaf*, and al-Bayhaqi, in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, narrated from al-Zuhri that "Hafsah came to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, with a book of the stories of Yusuf written on a shoulder-blade, and she began to read it to him, while the Prophet, peace be upon him, saw his face change colour. He said: 'By Him in whose hand my soul is, if Yusuf himself came to you and I were among you, and you followed him and abandoned me, you would have gone astray. I am your portion of the prophets, and you are my portion of the nations.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi also narrated from Abu Qilabah that "'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by a man reading a book, and he listened to it for a while and admired it. He said to the man: 'Write for me a copy of this book.' The man said: 'Yes.' So he bought a piece of leather, prepared it, and brought it to him, and he copied it for him on its front and back. Then he came to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and began to read it to him, and the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed colour. A man from the Ansar struck the book and said: 'May your mother be bereft of you, son of al-Khattab! Do you not see the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ since today, while you read this book to him?' Then the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said at that: 'I have only been sent as one who opens and seals, I have been given concise comprehensive words and their conclusions, and the speech has been abridged for me. Let not those who are bewildered (al-mutahawwikun) destroy you.'"

That is, those who fall into every matter without deliberation. It has also been said that they are those who are confused by such reports. Some scholars investigated and concluded that the prohibition applies only when there is fear of corruption in the religion, and there is no doubt about this in the early period of Islam. The reports are to be understood in this light, and the discussion of this has already passed, so recall it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 52:

﴿Say: "Sufficient is God as a witness between me and you."﴾ That is, knowing what proceeded from me of conveying and warning, and what proceeded from you of confronting me with denial and rejection. So He, glorified is He, will recompense each according to what befits him. ﴿He knows whatever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, of the matters among which are my affair and your affair. So this is a confirmation of what precedes it, namely His sufficiency as a witness, may He be exalted. It has also been allowed that the meaning is: Sufficient is He, mighty and majestic, as a witness to my truthfulness, that is, one who confirms me in what I claim through the miracles, as a witness confirms the claim of a claimant. The clause ( يَعْلَمُ ) ("He knows") is either a qualifier of ( شَهِيدًا ) ("witness") or a circumstantial clause, or a resumptive clause giving the reason for His sufficiency. It has been said against this: this interpretation is not suited by His exalted words ( بَيْنِي وبَيْنَكم ) ("between me and you"), whether it is connected to ( كَفى ) ("sufficient") or to ( شَهِيدًا ), nor by His glorified words ( يَعْلَمُ ما في السَّماواتِ ) ("He knows whatever is in the heavens") etc. There is room for reflection on this.

This may be supported by what has been narrated: "Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions said: 'O Muhammad, who will testify that you are the Messenger of God?' So the verse ﴿Say, sufficient...﴾ was revealed."

However, there is something in the heart about the soundness of this narration, because the context and the preceding and following passages concern the disbelievers of Quraysh, so do not be heedless.

Whatever the case, there is no contradiction between this verse and His exalted words: ﴿And call your witnesses besides God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], on the basis that the meaning is: do not seek testimony by God, and do not say "God, exalted is He, testifies that what we claim is true," as the one incapable of establishing proof says. This is either because the witness here means the knower, and the statement is a promise and a threat, or it means the one who confirms through the miracles, and testimony is not one of the two meanings there. The ba' in ( بِاللَّهِ ) ("by God") is superfluous (zā'idah), and the august Name is the subject of ( كَفى ) ("sufficient"). Al-Zajjaj said: "The ba' entered in order to imply in kafā the meaning of iktafi (be content/suffice), so the ba' is, as al-Laqqani said, transitive (mu'addiyah), not superfluous." Ibn Hisham said in al-Mughni: "This is in a very good position. It is confirmed by their saying: 'Whoever fears God, exalted is He, a man who did good will be rewarded for it,' meaning: let him fear, as shown by the jussive of yuthab ('will be rewarded'). It also requires it, their saying: 'Kafā bi-Hindin' ('Hind is sufficient'), with the omission of the tā'." [Page 8]

If it is objected by the intervening word, it is permissible but not obligatory, as shown by: ﴿And not a leaf falls﴾. If it is countered by "Ahsan bi-Hind" (the ba' with an elative), then the tā' does not attach to the forms of the imperative, even if their meaning is informative. End of quotation.

Al-Shaykh Yasin al-Himsi commented on this in his glosses on al-Tasrih, saying: "I say: interpreting ( كَفى ) according to this view as iktafi is not correct, since the subject of ( كَفى ) in that case is a pronoun of the addressee, and ( كَفى ) is a past-tense verb, and it does not raise a concealed pronoun of the addressee." End of quotation. There is in it a distance of inquiry that is not hidden from the reflective.

Some people thought that ( كَفى ) according to this view is an imperative verbal noun (ism fi'l amr) addressed to the singular masculine and others, like ( حَيَّ ) in ( حَيَّ عَلى الصَّلاةِ ) ("come to prayer"). So the meaning here is: "Be content with God." You know that this is far from the intention of al-Zajjaj's statement, and the statement of Ibn Hisham rejects it. Ibn al-Sarraj said: the subject is a pronoun of the act of being content. Ibn Hisham said: the soundness of his statement depends on the permissibility of a preposition being connected to the pronoun of the verbal noun (maṣdar). This is the view of al-Farisi and al-Rummani, who permitted: "My passing by Zayd is good, and passing by 'Amr is ugly." The Kufans permitted its operation on adverbs of place and others, while the majority of the Basrans prohibited its operation absolutely. End of quotation.

Ibn al-Sa'igh responded to this, saying: "We do not accept that soundness depends on that, because the ba' may be for the state (ḥāl), and in that case the meaning is: ( كَفى ) is the act of being content (ī al-iktifā') while being connected to God, exalted is He. It is not hidden that as long as this view is not invalidated, what Ibn Hisham claimed is not complete, namely that omitting the tā' in 'Kafā bi-Hindin' requires that kafā be implied with the meaning of iktafi. So reflect."

﴿And those who believed in falsehood﴾. Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: that is, in other than God, mighty and majestic is He. This includes such as Jesus and the angels, peace be upon them.

Falsehood in reality is their worship, and falsehood here is not like it in the words of Hassan:

"Surely everything other than God is vain."

Muqatil said:

That is, by the worship of Satan. It was also said: that is, by the idol. ﴿And disbelieved in God﴾, despite the convergence of the requirements of belief in Him, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿Those are the losers﴾, the defrauded in their transaction, since they exchanged disbelief for belief, and thus deserved punishment on the Day of Reckoning. It has been said that in the speech there is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah): the exchange of disbelief for belief, which entails punishment, is likened to a purchase that entails loss. In "loss" there is an imaginative metaphor (isti'arah takhyiliyyah), which is its indicator, because loss is customary in trade. This statement comes in the manner of fairness, since it did not explicitly state that they are those who believe in falsehood and disbelieve in God, mighty and majestic is He, but rather presented it in the form of generality, so that reflection might arrive at the sought matter directly. It is like His exalted words: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance, or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24], and like the words of Hassan:

"So let your evil be the ransom of your good."

This is of the kind of disputation in the best manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 53:

﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾, i.e., the disbelievers of Quraysh ask you to hasten the punishment ﴿bi-l-adhab﴾, in a manner of mockery, challenge and denial of it, by their saying: (When is this promise?) and their saying: Rain down upon us stones, or bring us a punishment, and the like. ﴿Had it not been for a term appointed﴾, which Allah, exalted is He, has set for their punishment and named, and fixed in the Preserved Tablet, ﴿the punishment would have come upon them﴾, specified for them in accordance with what they hastened for. Ibn Salam said: it refers to the interval between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). It was also said: it refers to the Day of Badr. It was also said: it refers to the time of their perishing at their appointed terms, and this has an obvious weakness, since they were not promised their natural death, nor were they hastening for it. ﴿And it will surely come upon them﴾: this is a resumptive clause explaining what was indicated in the preceding clause concerning the coming of the punishment when the term arrives, i.e., by Allah, exalted is He, the punishment designated for them will surely come upon them at the arrival of the term ﴿suddenly﴾.

i.e., unexpectedly ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, i.e., its coming. Perhaps what is meant by its coming in this way is that it does not occur through hastening in response to their urgency and the granting of their request, for that would be a coming in accordance with their opinion and awareness. Rather, it comes upon them while they are settled and secure, not expecting it at all, as is the custom of some punishments that descended upon some nations by night while they were sleeping, or in the forenoon while they were playing. This is because the coming of the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of the Day of Badr is not of this kind, as said by some of them. ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, and indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new clause that begins a fresh statement), brought to show the extent of their ignorance and the feebleness of their opinion. It is evident that what they asked to be hastened is the punishment of the Hereafter. The clause ﴿indeed Hell...﴾ and so on, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they ask you to hasten the punishment, while the place of the punishment, beyond which there is no punishment, encompasses them. It is as if it were said: they ask you to hasten the punishment, and indeed the punishment encompasses them, that is, it will encompass them, taking the active participle (ism al-fa'il) in the sense of the future; or it is as if it already encompasses them, because of the encompassing of disbelief and sins which bring it upon them. In the statement there is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), or a metaphor (isti'arah), or a metonymy (majaz mursal), or a figurative attribution (tajawwuz fi al-isnad). It has been said: disbelief and sins are in reality the Fire, but they appear in this world in this form. The intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is those who ask for the hastening. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate the cause of the ruling, or it refers to the category of disbelievers, and those who asked for the hastening are included in it by primary inclusion.

The verse "on the Day the punishment will cover them" (﴿يَوْمَ يَغْشاهُمُ العَذابُ﴾): the phrase "on the Day" (ẓarf, an adverb of time) modifies an implied verb that has been omitted, to signal the extreme magnitude and horror of that Day. It is as if it were said: "on the Day that the punishment comes upon them and envelops them, the punishment mentioned in the statement of Hell's encompassing them, there will be states and terrors that speech cannot express." It was also said that the adverb of time modifies (muḥīṭah, "encompassing"), meaning: "Indeed, Hell will encompass the disbelievers on the Day the punishment covers them." ﴿مِن فَوْقِهِمْ ومِن تَحْتِ أرْجُلِهِمْ﴾ ("from above them and from beneath their feet"), that is, from all their directions. What is mentioned here is for generality, as in "in the mornings and the evenings" (al-ghuduww wa al-āṣāl). It was said that the mention of the feet indicates that they will have no rest and will not sit, and that this is the greatest of punishments. ﴿ويَقُولُ﴾ ("and He will say"), that is, Allah, Mighty and Majestic; it was also said that it is the angel assigned to them.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿĀmir and the Basran readers read "wa-naqūlu" (and We say) with the nun of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), which clearly indicates that the speaker is Allah, exalted is He.

Abu al-Barahsam read "wa-taqūlu" (and she says) with the letter tāʾ, meaning that the speaker is Hell. Speech is attributed to it here just as it is attributed to it in His saying: ﴿وتَقُولُ هَلْ مِن مَزِيدٍ﴾ ("and it will say: Is there any more?") [Qāf: 30]. Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn Abī ʿAblah read "wa-yuqālu" (and it is said) in the passive voice. ﴿ذُوقُوا ما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("Taste what you used to do"), that is, the recompense for what you used to do in the world continuously of evil deeds, among which is the hastening of the punishment.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 56:**

﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾

It was revealed, according to what is narrated from Muqatil and al-Kalbi, concerning the oppressed believers in Mecca, who were commanded to emigrate from it. Most exegetes (mufassirun) hold this view. Some of them generalized the ruling to everyone who cannot establish the affairs of the religion as they should in a land because of an obstacle from the disbelievers or others. So he said: emigration to a land where he can do that is obligatory upon him. This was also narrated from Ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', Mujahid, and Malik ibn Anas. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: the verse is a promise from Him, exalted is He, of abundant provision in the whole earth. According to both views, the word "earth" (ard) means the known earth.

(Page 10)

Al-Jubba'i said: the verse is a promise from Him, mighty and majestic is He, of admission into Paradise for whoever sincerely devotes worship to Him, glorified is He. He interpreted "earth" as the earth of Paradise. The reliable view is what has preceded.

The fa' in "fa-iyyaya" (so Me alone) is the fa' of causation (tasabbub), referring to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿indeed My earth is vast﴾.

This is like when you say: "Indeed Zayd is your brother, so honor him." Likewise, if you said: "Indeed he is your brother, so if you are able, then honor him." The word "iyyaya" (Me alone) is an object (ma'mul) of a verb that is omitted and explained by what is mentioned. It cannot be an object of the mentioned verb, because that verb is occupied by its pronoun. That omitted verb is the response (jaza') to a condition (shart) that was omitted, and this object was put in its place as a substitute. The fa' in "fa-u'buduni" (so worship Me) is the fa' that occurs in the response, but because its omission was obligatory, the explaining and emphasizing element was placed in its position verbally, and the fa' was attached to it, since the fa' is necessary to indicate the response. It is not attached to the object of the omitted verb, namely "iyyaya." Even if it were supposed to be free of the fa', because it has become purely a substitute for the conditional verb, the attachment to the explainer is required. Also, so that the mentioned matches the omitted in every respect. It is necessary that the omitted verb governing "iyyaya" be estimated as delayed, so that the substitution for the conditional verb is not lost, while this also conveys the meaning of exclusivity (ikhtisas) and sincerity (ikhlas). So the meaning is: indeed My earth is vast; so if you do not sincerely devote worship to Me in one land, then devote it to Me in another. He made the condition "if you do not sincerely devote" because the mentioned response indicates it.

There is no objection to the first fa' being the response to another condition, reinforcing the causal sense in the meaning that "indeed My earth is vast." In that case the meaning is: if you do not sincerely devote worship to Me, etc. It has also been said: the first fa' is the response to an estimated condition, while the second is a repetition so that the explainer matches the explained. Then the meaning is: indeed My earth is vast, if you do not sincerely devote worship to Me in one land, then devote it to Me in another. The estimated conditional clause, namely "if you do not sincerely devote, etc.," is then a new clause free of the fa'. But what has preceded is more remote in its purpose.

Some verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) made the second fa' a coordinating fa' linking what follows to the estimated governing element of "iyyaya," intentionally for a sense of comprehensiveness, as in: "take the best, then the better." It was objected that in that case the mentioned cannot serve as an explainer, because it is absolutely impermissible for a coordinating particle to intervene between an explainer and what is explained. As for what Imam al-Sakkaki mentioned concerning the verse ﴿so Me alone, fear Me﴾ [al-Nahl: 51], that the fa' is coordinating and the estimate is: "so Me alone, fear; fear Me," he meant that it is so originally, not in its present state, as verified by the author of al-Kashf. Scholars have prolonged the discussion on this point, and we have mentioned a portion of it at the beginning of the tafsir of Surat al-Baqarah, so return to it together with what is here, and reflect. And God, exalted is He, is the Guide to the straight path.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 57:

﴿Every soul shall taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾ This is a resumed (mustaʼnafah) sentence, brought in to urge sincerity in worship and migration (hijrah) for the sake of God Most High, since it conveys that this world is not a place of permanence and that behind it lies the abode of recompense. That is: every soul among souls is certain to experience the bitterness of death and to separate from the body without exception, so you will inevitably taste it, and then you will be returned to Our judgment and Our recompense according to your deeds. Whoever has this as his end must therefore prepare and equip himself with provision. In God's words (ذائِقَةُ المَوْتِ, "tasting death"), there is a metaphor (istiʻarah) that likens death to something of bitter and disagreeable taste. The shift away from saying "tasting death" in another form serves to indicate certainty (al-tahaqquq). ("Thumma," "then") denotes temporal sequence (li-l-tarakhi al-zamani) or sequence in rank (al-rutbi).

Abu Haywah read ذائِقَةٌ with tanwin and المَوْتَ with the accusative. ʻAli, may God honor his face, read تَرْجِعُونَ with the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). Asim transmitted يَرْجِعُونَ with the third-person yaʼ.

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will surely settle them﴾, i.e., We will surely make them dwell (lanunzilannahum) in the manner of residence. The phrase of the oath and its answer is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada', i.e., the inchoative), namely ( alladhina ). By this and similar examples, Tha'lab, who prevented an oath clause and the sworn-about clause from being the predicate of a subject, was refuted. His (exalted) saying ﴿from the Garden, chambers﴾ means lofty chambers and magnificent palaces with no defect in them. According to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, they are of pearls, chrysolite, and rubies. It is the second object (maf'ul thani) of the verb tabwi'a (to settle).
