'Ali, may God ennoble his face, 'Abdullah, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "lanuthawwiyannahum" with the unvowelled (sakin) thaʾ after the nun, and the hamza changed to yāʾ, from al-thawa' meaning residence. In that case, the accusative of ﴿chambers﴾ is either because it is treated as (the object of) lanunzilannahum, so it is a direct object (maf'ul bihi); or by removing the preposition, the original being "bi-ghuraf," and when the preposition is deleted, it takes the accusative; or it is an adverb (zarf), and an adverb of place, when definite like "the house" or "the room," cannot be put in the accusative as an adverb except that here it is treated as indefinite for the sake of extension (tawassu'an), as in His (exalted) saying ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [Al-A'raf: 16], as detailed in grammar.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he read "ghurufan" with a damma on the ra' ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ is a qualifier of (ghurafan). ﴿Abiding therein﴾, i.e., in the chambers; and it was said: in the Garden. ﴿How excellent is the reward of the doers﴾, i.e., of the righteous deeds. The thing praised is omitted, relying on the indication of what precedes it, i.e., "how excellent is the reward of the doers: the chambers," or "their reward." It is permissible for the specification (tamyiz) to be omitted, i.e., "how excellent a reward is the reward of the doers." Ibn Wathhab read "fa-ni'ma" with the fa' of sequence.

Ruh al-Ma'ani (al-Alusi), on Surah 29, verse 59:

﴿Those who were patient﴾ is a qualifying description (sifah) of "those who do righteous deeds," or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), or it is in the accusative case (nusiba) by way of praise (madh), meaning: they were patient under the harm of the polytheists, the hardships of emigration (muhajarah), and other trials and difficulties; ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾, meaning: in what they undertake and what they leave undone, they relied on none but Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 60:

﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision! God provides for it and for you﴾. This is according to what has been related: that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the believers who were in Makkah to emigrate to Madinah, and they said: "How can we go to a town where we have no livelihood?" Then this was revealed.

That is: and how many a creature there is that cannot bear carrying its provision because of its weakness, or does not store it, and so it rises in the morning with no livelihood with it. From Ibn ʿUyayna: "There is nothing that hoards except man, the ant and the mouse." From Ibn ʿAbbas: "None stores except the human, the ant, the mouse and the magpie (ʿaqʿaq)." It is said that the magpie is called mukhabi, except that it forgets where it has hidden things. From some of them: "I saw the nightingale (bulbul) hoarding in its lap (ḥiḍnayhi)," but the apparent meaning is that this is not sound. Some people mentioned to me that most of the birds that peck (al-kawamin min al-tayr) do store, and God the Exalted knows best its soundness.

﴿God provides for it and for you﴾. Then, although it is weak and trusts in God, and you, despite your strength and striving, are equal in that none provides for it and for you except God the Exalted, because the provision of all is through means, but He, mighty and majestic, is alone the One who causes it. So do not fear for your livelihood through emigration. And since the aim was to remove what was in their imaginations about emigration in the most emphatic manner, it was said: ﴿provides for it and for you﴾ rather than "provides for you and for it." ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾, who is perfect in hearing, so He hears this your saying, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, who is perfect in knowledge, so He knows what your hearts conceal.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 61:

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ That is, the people of Makkah. For they have no way to deny this or to waver about it. The noble Name (Allah) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted, the question indicating it; or it is in the nominative as an agent (fa'il) of a verb omitted for the same reason. ﴿Then how are they turned away?﴾ This is a rebuke and a expression of astonishment from Him, exalted is He, at their abandoning the act that its requirement demands. The fa' (then) denotes sequence, or it falls in the answer of an implied conditional clause, meaning: if the matter is so, how are they diverted from acknowledging His singularity in divinity, given their acknowledgment of His singularity in what was mentioned of creation and subjection?

Some of them supposed the conditional clause, "then if desire and Satan divert them," on account of the form of (yu'faku) being in the passive voice. And what we have mentioned is perhaps more preferable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 62:

﴿Allah expands provision for whom He wills among His servants and restricts it for him﴾: that is, He expands it for him and for no one else. ﴿And restricts it for him﴾: that is, He constricts it for him. The pronoun refers to ( whom He wills ), the one for whom He expands provision. That is, it refers to him while keeping in view its complement (the restriction). The meaning, then, is that He, exalted is His majesty, expands provision for one particular person at one time and restricts it for him at another. The waw (و) denotes mere joining, so restriction may come before expansion. Alternatively, the pronoun refers to ( whom He wills ) without regard to its complement, so that what is meant is another person, other than the one previously mentioned. This is like the saying: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning half of another dirham. This is close to what is called al-istikhdam (a rhetorical device in which a single expression is used with two different referents). The meaning, then, is that He, exalted is His majesty, expands provision for some people and restricts it for others.

Ibn Amir ... ʿAlqama read ﴿ويُقَدِّرُ﴾ (wa-yuqaddiru) with a damma on the ya, a fatha on the qaf, and a shadda on the dal. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾: so He knows that each of expansion and restriction, at whatever time, accords with wisdom and benefit, and He does each of them at its proper time. Or, He knows who is fit for the expansion of provision, and so He expands it for him, and who is fit for its restriction, and so He restricts it for him. This verse, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah expands﴾ and so on, completes the meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Allah provides for it and for you﴾, because the first is a statement about the one provided for and its generality, while this is a statement about provision and its expansion and its constriction.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah al-'Ankabut (29), verse 63:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if you ask them﴾, etc., is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) serving to reinforce the meaning of the two verses, and an allusion (ta'rid) that those on whom you relied for sustenance acknowledge Our power and Our might, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 58]. This was said by the scholar al-Tibi.

The author of al-Kashshaf, may his secret be sanctified, said: A parenthetical clause is inserted to indicate that the Creator is the Provider, and that the One who bestows and brings into existence at the outset is more worthy of being able to sustain. By it he reinforced what was contained in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾.

﴿And if you ask them who sends down water from the sky and with it revives the earth after its death, they will surely say, "Allah."﴾ They acknowledge that He, mighty and majestic is He, is the One who brings into existence all possible things, their roots and their branches. Yet they associate with Him, glorified is He, some of His creatures from whom one can hardly imagine any power over anything at all. ﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah"﴾ for the establishing of the proof and their acknowledgment of what is incumbent upon them. It has been said that the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him praised Him for safeguarding him from the error in which they were, since they associated others with Him while acknowledging that the roots of blessings and their branches come from Him, may His majesty be exalted. This is then like praise on seeing one who is afflicted. It has also been said that it may be praise for this and for that.

﴿But most of them do not understand﴾ what they say, and what it contains of indication of the falsehood of polytheism and the soundness of monotheism; or they do not understand anything at all, and therefore they do not act in accordance with the requirement of this statement of theirs, so they associate with Him, glorified is He, the lowliest of His creatures. It has been said that this is a turning away (idrab) from their particular ignorance in bringing forth what is a proof against them, to the point that this is because they are deprived of intellect, so it is not far from them that such a thing should occur. His exalted saying: (Say: "Praise be to Allah") is a parenthetical clause. Al-Zamakhshari, in Surah Luqman, took it as an obligation and an affirmation of His exalted entitlement to worship. It has also been said: (they do not understand) what you intend by praising Him at their saying that; but some of the verifiers did not accept this, due to its obscurity, its little benefit, and the strained application of the turning away in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 64:

﴿وما هَذِهِ الحَياةُ الدُّنْيا﴾ — "And this worldly life" is an expression of belittling; and how could it not be, since the world does not weigh with Allah the Exalted the wing of a gnat.

For al-Tirmidhi narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If the world were worth to Allah the Exalted the wing of a gnat, He would not have given a disbeliever a single sip of water from it.'"

And some of the knowers of Allah said: "The world is more worthless than the foreleg of a dead pig over which a dog has urinated, in the hand of a leper." From what has been mentioned, the worthlessness of the life that is in it is known all the more so. ﴿إلا لَهْوٌ ولَعِبٌ﴾ — "except amusement and play," that is, except as children amuse themselves and play with a thing, gathering around it and rejoicing in it for a while, then dispersing from it. This is an eloquent simile.

﴿وإنَّ الدّارَ الآخِرَةَ لَهي الحَيَوانُ﴾ — "And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter, that is the true life," that is, it is the abode of true life, since death and annihilation do not befall those who are in it; or it is itself life, for emphasis. (Al-Hayawan) is a verbal noun of "hayiya" (to live), which is used for the living being in other than this context. Its original form is "hayayan," and the second yā' was changed into wāw contrary to analogy, so its final radical is yā'; this is the view of Sibawayh.

It has been said that its final radical is wāw, taking into account the apparent form of the word, and (the name) Hayah is the name of a man. There is no proof that it is yā' in "hayy" (living), because the wāw in such a pattern is changed to yā' due to the kasra before it, as in "shaqiyy" from "al-shiqwa" (wretchedness). It is more eloquent than "al-hayah" (life), because the pattern fa'alan carries the meaning of movement and agitation which is inherent to life; and for this reason it was chosen over it in this context, which calls for emphasis. You have already known it in the description of the worldly life, which is contrasted with the Hereafter.

﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ — "if they only knew." This is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, meaning: if they knew, they would not have preferred over it the world, whose origin is the absence of life, and then what occurs in it of life is an accident swift to vanish and quick to dissolve. That "law" (lau) here indicates wishing is far-fetched.

﴿When they board the ship﴾ is connected to what is implied by the description of their condition. Rukub (riding, boarding) means being raised above a moving thing, and it is transitive by itself, as in ﴿that you may ride upon them﴾ [An-Nahl: 8]. Its use here and in similar contexts is a negation, to signal that the vessel in itself belongs to the category of places, and that its motion is compelled and not voluntary. The fa' (then) denotes sequence, and the sentence carries the sense of a limit (ghayah). It is as if it were said: they are diverted from the Tawhid of God, Exalted is He, despite acknowledging what it requires, heedless of that which passes quickly, and oblivious of eternal life, until, when they board the ship and encounter hardships, ﴿they call upon God, sincerely devoting religion to Him﴾, meaning they are in the form of those who made their religion, their creed, or their obedience sincere among the believers, since they mention none but God Exalted, and call upon none other than Him, Glorified is He, knowing that none removes hardships except Him, Mighty and Majestic. In this there is also mockery of them, whether by "religion" is meant the creed or obedience. As for the first, it is evident; as for the second, it is because they do not persist in this state, so it is ugly in its outcome. ﴿But when He delivered them safely to the land, behold, they associate partners with Him﴾, meaning they hastened to return to polytheism, and did not delay in it even for a moment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 66:

﴿لِيَكْفُرُوا بِما آتَيْناهم ولِيَتَمَتَّعُوا﴾ The apparent meaning is that the lam in both places is the lam of purpose (lam kay), i.e., they associate partners with Allah so that they may be ungrateful for what We have given them, namely the blessing of deliverance, because of their shirk; and so that they may enjoy themselves through their gathering together in the worship of idols and their mutual affection over them. Thus shirk is the cause of this ingratitude, and the lam of purpose has been placed before its result, making it as though it were their aim from it. Therefore it is, in reality, the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah). It has also been said that the lam in both places is the lam of command (lam al-amr), and that the command to be ungrateful and to enjoy themselves is metaphorical, expressing abandonment (al-takhliyah), forsaking (al-khidhlan), and threat (al-tahdid), as you say in anger to someone who opposes you: "Do whatever you wish." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i, "wa-liyatamatta'u" with a sukun on the lam, since the lam of purpose is not vowelled with a sukun. If the second lam is the lam of command, then the first is like it, so that the coordination (al-'atf) is clear. Their difference requires far-fetched interpretation, namely, as Abu Hayyan said, that the meaning is coordination of one statement upon another (atf kalam 'ala kalam), not coordination of one verb upon another verb. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("So they will soon know"), i.e., the outcome of that when they are requited for it on the Day of Resurrection, confirms the threat.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 67:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ that is, have they not looked and not witnessed? ﴿That We have made﴾ i.e., their city ﴿a sanctuary (haram)﴾, a place in which many things are forbidden that are not forbidden in other places ﴿secure (amin)﴾, its people safe from what would harm them, such as capture and killing. This is on the basis that its security is a metonymy for the security of its people; or on the basis that the attribution is metaphorical (majazi); or on the basis that there is an omitted genitive (mudaf muqaddar) in the sentence. The specification of the people of Mecca, and that the security extends to everyone within it, even the birds and the beasts, is because the intended purpose is to bestow favour upon them, and because this security is continuous with regard to them.

Juwaybir narrated, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: "The people of Mecca said: O Muhammad, what prevents us from entering your religion is only our fear that people will snatch us away, because we are few and the Arabs are more numerous than us. So whenever it reaches them that we have entered your religion, we will be snatched away, for we are all a morsel (akalat ra's, i.e., easy prey). Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Have they not seen that We have made a sanctuary secure,﴾
Page 14
﴿while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾"

Yukhtalasun min hawlihim qatlan wa sabyan (they are plundered from around them by killing and captivity), when the Arabs around it were in raiding and pillaging. The apparent reading is that the sentence is a circumstantial clause (haliyya) with an implied subject (mubtada'), i.e., "while they are being snatched away," etc. ﴿Then in falsehood do they believe?﴾ That is, after the manifestation of the truth about which there is no doubt, or after this manifest blessing and others, do they believe in the idol? And it has been said: they believe in Satan. ﴿And in the blessing of Allah do they disbelieve?﴾ That is, the blessing that deserves gratitude, in that they associate with Him, glory be to Him, other than Him. The placing of the relative clause (sila) first in both places is for emphasis upon it, because it is the object of the denunciation, or for restriction by way of exaggeration, since belief that is not exclusive is not counted as belief, and because ingratitude toward other than His blessing, in comparison with ingratitude toward it, is not considered ingratitude.

Al-Sulami and al-Hasan read *tu'minun* and *takfurun* with the second-person (taa' al-khitab) in both places.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 29, verse 68:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ by claiming that He, glory be to Him, has a partner. That this is a lie against Allah the Exalted is because it concerns Him; it is like your saying "He lied against Zayd" when he describes him with what is not in him. ﴿Or denies the truth﴾, meaning the Messenger or the Book, ﴿when it has come to him﴾, i.e., at the time of its coming to him. In this there is a rebuke of them, since they did not reflect and did not pause when it came to them, but rather hastened to deny it the moment they heard it.

﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling place for the disbelievers?﴾ That is, a place of abode and residence for them, or a place where they dwell and remain. The statement on both interpretations is an affirmation of their dwelling in Hell, because the interrogative here carries the sense of negation, and it has entered upon a negation, and the negation of a negation is an affirmation, as in the verse of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who have ridden mounts, and the most generous of the worlds in giving wine?"

That is: do they not deserve to dwell, or the place in which they dwell therein? They have fabricated a similar lie against Allah the Exalted, and denied the truth with a similar denial. Or it is a denunciation and a deeming-far of their audacity in what has been mentioned of fabrication and denial, along with their knowledge of the state of the disbelievers; that is, did they not know that in Hell there is a dwelling place for the disbelievers, such that they dared this boldness? He made them as those who know this, because it is clear and manifest, so they were treated as those who know it. The definiteness in "the disbelievers" on the first interpretation is for previous mention (al-'ahd), so what is meant is those spoken of, namely the people of Mecca. The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun to give the cause for their deserving the dwelling place. This does not conflict with the apparent meaning that the cause is their fabrication and denial, because it is not different from it, and causation admits of multiplicity. On the second interpretation, the definiteness is generic (lil-jins), so what is meant is the whole category of disbelievers, and those people enter into it by way of primary, evident inclusion.

[p. 14]

﴿And those who strive for Us﴾: for Our sake, for Our cause, and seeking Our Face sincerely. There is an implied noun here, meaning "for the sake of Our cause." It was also said that no such implied word is needed, since the statement can be taken as hyperbole, making Allah's Essence the place where striving settles. The word "striving" is used in a general sense to include striving against enemies, both outward and inward, in all their kinds. ﴿We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾: the paths of journeying toward Us and arriving at Our presence. What is meant is that We will increase them in guidance to the paths of good and grant them success in following them, for striving is either a form of guidance or is consequent upon it. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17]. A hadith also states: "Whoever acts on what he knows, Allah will bequeath to him the knowledge of what he did not know."

Some people have interpreted "strived" (jahadu) as "intended striving," and kept ﴿We will surely guide them﴾ on its apparent meaning. Al-Suddi said: the meaning is, "Those who strive by steadfastness in faith, We will surely guide them to Our paths, which lead to Paradise." It was also said: the meaning is, "Those who strive in battle, We will surely guide them to the paths of martyrdom and forgiveness." The first interpretation is preferable. The relative pronoun is the subject (mubtada'), and the oath with its answer is the predicate (khabar), like the similar statement earlier: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty chambers in Paradise﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 58].

[p. 15]

﴿And indeed Allah﴾, who is characterized by all the attributes of perfection, whose greatness has reached the hearts to whatever extent it has, ﴿is surely with the doers of good﴾, with the companionship of support and help. The mention of striving, which requires these two, is a strong indication of this meaning. The scholar al-Tibi said: Allah's statement ﴿is surely with the doers of good﴾ corresponds with His statement "strived" (jahadu) both in wording and meaning. As for the wording, it corresponds in the unrestricted use of striving and companionship. As for the meaning, the one who strives against enemies needs a helper and supporter. Furthermore, the sentence of the Mighty and Majestic's statement ﴿Indeed Allah is surely with the doers of good﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the verse, emphasized with two words of emphasis and given the Name of the Essence, to indicate that whoever strives with his whole being and innermost self for the sake of the One who is exalted, the Lord, whose name is Majestic, all-comprehensive in the attribute of support and aid, will manifest Himself to him completely. Moreover, this is a noble conclusion to the surah, because it answers its opening and looks to its unique necklace-pearl: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 2], and it alludes to the central pearl of its necklace: ﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 56]. It is itself a comprehensive and unique unit. End of quotation.

The "al-" in "the doers of good" (al-muhsinin) may be the definite article of prior reference (al-'ahd), so that "the doers of good" means those who strove. The reason for using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun is clear, and this is the view of the majority. It may also be the article of genus, so that "the doers of good" means anyone who does good deeds in general, and those mentioned enter this group first and foremost, by proof. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he interpreted "the doers of good" as "the monotheists" (al-muwahhidin). This supports the second possibility. And Allah knows best.

* * *

From the allusive (ishari) interpretation of the verses: regarding ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone...﴾ up to the verse, Ibn 'Ata' said: Creation assumed that they would be left alone with claims of love, and would not be tested regarding its realities. These realities are pouring affliction upon the lover, and his delight in outward and inward affliction. This is like what the gnostic Ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified, said:

"Your punishment is sweet to me, and your injustice upon me is justice, in accordance with what desire decrees for you."

They mentioned that love and trial are twins, and "a man is honored or humiliated through testing." ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for Allah's sake, he regards people's persecution as Allah's punishment﴾ is an allusion to the state of those who lie in claiming love, who are turned away from it by people's harm to them. ﴿Indeed, those you worship besides Allah have no power to provide you with sustenance. So seek sustenance from Allah, worship Him, give thanks to Him. To Him you will be returned﴾. Ibn 'Ata' said: That is, seek provision through obedience and devotion to worship. Sahl said: seek it in trust in God (tawakkul), not in earning, for seeking provision by earning is the way of the common folk. ﴿And he said, "Indeed I am migrating to my Lord"﴾, that is, I am migrating from my self and from created existence toward Him, the Mighty and Majestic. Ibn 'Ata' said: that is, I am returning to my Lord from all that is mine and upon me. Returning to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, comes through separation from whatever is other than Him, the Glorified. Returning to Allah the Exalted is not valid for anyone while he is attached to anything in existence; rather, he must separate himself from all created existences. ﴿And you commit an abomination in your gatherings﴾: al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, was asked about this verse, and he said: "Everything that people gather for is abominable except remembrance (dhikr) of Allah."

﴿The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that makes itself a house, and indeed the frailest of houses is the spider's house﴾. He, glorified and exalted, indicated those who rely on other than Allah the Mighty and Majestic in the means of this world and the Hereafter. Such a person is cut off from his goal and does not reach it. Ibn 'Ata' said: whoever relies on anything other than Allah the Exalted, his destruction will be in the very thing he relied upon. Whoever takes other than Him, the Mighty and Majestic, as a helper, cuts himself off from the path of protection and is returned to his own power and strength.

﴿And these parables We set forth for people, but none understands them except those who have knowledge﴾. In this there is an allusion that the subtleties of knowledge are known only by the people of spiritual states who know Him, the Exalted, His attributes, and all His affairs, glorified be He, because they are the scholars of the method. It is mentioned that the true scholar is one whose knowledge restrains him from everything that outward knowledge permits. This is the one whose intellect is supported by the lights of divinely bestowed knowledge (al-'ilm al-ladunni). ﴿Indeed, prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing﴾. It is mentioned that the reality of prayer is the presence of the heart in the manner of remembrance, and vigilance in the manner of reflection. Remembrance in prayer drives away heedlessness, which is indecency, and reflection drives away blameworthy thoughts, which are wrongdoing. This is during prayer. After it, prayer restrains if it is a true prayer, which is the one in which the splendor of majesty and the grandeur of the heavenly kingdom are revealed to its owner, and his eyes are refreshed by witnessing the lights of the Truth, the Majestic and Exalted, beyond seeing deeds and rewards. Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: When prayer is accepted, it restrains one from contemplating deeds and rewards.

﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾. Ibn 'Ata' said: that is, Allah's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him, glorified be He, because His remembrance is without cause, while your remembrance is mixed with causes, hopes, and requests. Also, His remembrance is His attribute, and your remembrance is your attribute. There is no comparison between the attribute of the Creator, exalted is His majesty, and the attribute of the created. How far is dust from the Lord of lords! ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge﴾. In this there is an allusion that the brides of the realities of the Qur'an are revealed only to the spirits of those brought near among the gnostics and the divine scholars, because they are the places of the secrets of the divine attributes and the receptacles of the subtleties of the unveilings of the Essence. Al-Sadiq, upon his fathers and upon him be peace, said: Allah the Exalted has manifested Himself in His Book to His servants, but they do not perceive.

﴿O My servants who believe, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone﴾.

Sahl said: If sins and innovations are practiced in a land, then leave it for a land of the obedient. It seems this is so that the darkness of the disobedient's sins not be reflected onto the hearts of the obedient, causing them to become lazy in obedience. They mentioned that the traveling of the seeker is a cause of emptying and filling (of the self). To this refers what al-Tabarani, al-Qada'i, al-Khatib, al-Shirazi in al-Alqab, al-Khatib, Ibn al-Najjar, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Travel and you will be healthy and you will gain. Every soul shall taste death, so let not the fear of death prevent you from traveling." (ﷺ) ﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it and for you﴾: so let not the lack of provisions or inability to carry them prevent you from it.

﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾. Ibn 'Ata' said: that is, those who strive for Our pleasure, We will surely guide them to the place of pleasure. Striving, as he said, is turning in need to Allah the Exalted by severing oneself from everything other than Him. Some of them said: that is, those who occupy their outward selves with duties, We will surely connect their inward secrets to subtleties. It was also said: that is, those who strive against their souls for Our sake and seeking Us, We will surely guide them to the paths of knowing Us and arriving at Us. Whoever knows Allah the Exalted knows everything, and whoever arrives at Him finds everything easy. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak used to say: whoever finds a question difficult should ask the people of the frontiers about it, because of Allah's saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾. Striving against the self is the greatest striving. We ask Allah the Exalted for success in what He loves and is pleased with, and complete protection from every evil, by the sanctity of His beloved, the master of mankind, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him.
